Now the matter of the thirteen attributes is settled, and according to both this one and that one, the Sefirot are never anything but ten. However, regarding the question they asked the Gaon — whether the thirteen attributes are Sefirot or not — we have a proof that they are not an allusion to the Sefirot, in line with the Gaon's reasoning. And the proof is that they are called "thirteen attributes of mercy (rachamim)," yet among the Sefirot there are attributes of Din, such as Gevurah and Hod. Therefore, what is clear to us in this is that the thirteen attributes are the twelve boundaries (gevulin), which are the twelve [permutations of the four-letter] Name (havayot), and they are twelve; and the place that bears them, which is the Name that comprises them, [together they] are thirteen. And they are in each of three places, which are Teli, Galgal (sphere), and Lev (heart), and the mnemonic is "TaGeL" [TGL]. Besides which there are yet another thirteen [attributes] that are hidden, and they are in Keter. And what is fitting to elaborate in explaining this topic will be explained in the Gate of the Particulars of the Names, God willing, for there is its place, in the exposition of the seventy-two-[letter] Name.

Now Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah, peace be upon him, is [counted] among [those holding] this view, for he counted thirteen attributes in Keter, as I shall copy his words in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter 3, God willing. And likewise Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Idra wrote of thirteen attributes of mercy in Ze'eir Anpin and thirteen attributes in Arikh Anpin. It certainly appears that their view is the opposite of the Gaon's view, of blessed memory. And the exposition of the thirteen attributes does not belong here, for it will be explained in a book of its own, if God decrees [for me] life. And our purpose in this is to uphold the belief of the Kabbalists: that one must not believe in any addition to the ten Sefirot nor in any [number] less than them — for it is "a tent that shall not be moved, whose stakes shall not be pulled up" [Isaiah 33:20] — ten and not eleven; and one who adds or diminishes sins and brings evil upon himself. And of God we ask that He save us from errors.

After we have verified the matter of the number of the Sefirot, it is fitting that we investigate whether they are necessary from the standpoint of inquiry or not. To this we say that they are necessary for several reasons. The first: because we who believe in providence — and even in particular providence — are compelled to say that He exercises providence by way of the Sefirot. For the simple One, the Cause of all causes and the Cause of Causes, is removed from change and from attributes — that is, "wise," "righteous," "one who hears," and the rest of the predicates that the philosophers have removed from Him. So too the dimensions of body and corporeality, such as "And YHVH came down," and "And the appearance of the glory of YHVH was like a consuming fire," etc., and "And I saw YHVH sitting upon a throne," etc., and "And the glory of YHVH filled the Tabernacle," and "And they saw the God of Israel, and under His feet," etc., and what is said in Daniel (7:9), "And the Ancient of Days sat; His garment was white as snow," and likewise "written with the finger of God," "the ears of YHVH," "the hand of YHVH," "the eyes of YHVH" — matters of this kind that occur in Scripture indicating limit and corporeality, and likewise indicating predicates. Now of the simple One, in respect of its aspect relative to its very Self [atzmut] and its simplicity, it is impossible to say this — unless we consider it relative to its attributes, as we shall explain in the Gate of Self and Vessels and in the Gate of the Allusions, with the help of God.
And so it is by way of the attributes that the changes occur, and judgment and mercy — not in His [own] aspect — as will be explained in the aforementioned Gate.

Now from the standpoint of this aspect — so that we not deny the principles of our faith in the simple One, in the reality of its simplicity, that it is removed from the predicates that entail body and corporeal forms — and since we are compelled to believe in His providence, which too is among the principles of the religion, we therefore need to believe in the Sefirot, so that the principles of our faith not contradict one another, as explained. This, then, is a reason — or reasons — compelling belief in the Sefirot; and these are somewhat compelling proofs from the side of the Torah, by way of inquiry. However, by way of inquiry alone, without support and prop from the Torah, the commentators have written many further proofs; and because our way in this composition is not by way of inquiry, we have not copied them at all. Furthermore, these ten attributes — their secret and their import — have been expounded in Scripture. The first three are expounded from the words of Job to his companions, where he said (28:12), "But wisdom — whence shall it be found, and where is the place of understanding?" In this verse he set out for us the order of the first three, which are called Ayin (Nothing), Chokhmah, and Binah. First he said: Chokhmah is emanated from the first Sefirah, called Ayin, and this is "But wisdom — from Ayin (me-ayin) shall it be found." And A-Y — which is alef = Ayin, yod = Chokhmah — ZeH (this) is the place of Binah, [the place] by which Binah is emanated. But of the emanation of the Ayin he did not speak at all, for even the emanated is called Ayin (Nothing), all the more so the Emanator.

Now the seven [Sefirot] that proceed from them are expounded in the words of David, king of Israel, peace be upon him, in the verse (1 Chronicles 29:11): "Yours, O YHVH, is the greatness, and the power, and the beauty, and the victory, and the majesty; for all that is in heaven and on earth [is Yours]; Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom." The words "Yours, O YHVH" (lekha) are an epithet for the first three; and Binah is called lekha, which equals 50, like the count of the fifty gates of Binah. And the letters of L-KH (lekha) are the same as the letters of K-L (kol). And Yesod, when it receives from Binah the aforementioned fifty (nun) gates, is called KoL — like the image of the reversing seal, from L-KH to K-L. And the reason that the fifty gates are alluded to in the word lekha and in the word kol is that the gates are 50, in the secret of Binah, which spreads down to Hod — these being five Sefirot, each composed of ten, making fifty; and they are three over two: Gedulah-Gevurah-Tiferet (GGT) are a segol or segolta, which is 30; Netzach and Hod are a tzere or sheva, making 20 — thus L-KH (30+20) in their order. And KoL is in the secret of the reversing seal: what was above returned below. And the remaining matters of the gates will be explained in the Gate of Gates, with God's help. "The greatness" (ha-gedulah) is Chesed; "the power" (ha-gevurah) is Fear (Pachad); and then Tiferet, and Netzach, and Hod. "For all (kol) that is in heaven and on earth" — this is Yesod, the bond that binds heaven and earth. That is: it unifies Tiferet, called "heaven," and "earth," called Malkhut; and it is Yesod. And Malkhut was not clearly expounded in the verse; rather he said "Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom" — because Malkhut's place is above Netzach, Hod, and Yesod, and on account of [its] diminishment it descended below. Therefore he did not wish to mention it except by way of the unification, to indicate that its place is in heaven, save that it was cast from heaven to earth; and afterward he said "Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom," to set forth its hosts and its adornments in their own right; and even so he returned and unified it up to the supernal root, saying "Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom" — "Yours" [referring to] Binah, as explained. "YHVH" is Tiferet. "The kingdom" (mamlakhah) is Malkhut, in its plain sense. And this is its mode of existence together with its spouse — two kings nourished from a single Keter.

After we have occupied ourselves in the preceding chapters with the necessity of the existence of the Sefirot and their number, it is fitting that we know whether one who denies the matter of the existence of the Sefirot is called a heretic [kofer] or not. And we say that a person's error in this matter will be in one of two ways. The first way: one who did not know of them at all — not in the sense that, were the hidden things of wisdom revealed to him, he would deny them, God forbid, but [only] in the sense that he was not habituated to them and the gates of light were not revealed to him. This man certainly ought not to be called a heretic [kofer] or a denier. And a proof of this: for even regarding the removal of corporeality from the truly simple One, blessed be He, Rambam said, in Sefer ha-Mada, in the Laws of Repentance ch.3, that one who believes the simple One is a body and possessed of form is a sectarian [min], and he included him in the category of the sectarians (minim). And Ra'avad, peace be upon him, objected to him, and these are his words: "I say: and why did he call this one a sectarian? — when several great and good men greater than he went with this thought, according to what they saw in the Scriptures, and even more than what they saw in the words of the aggadot, which confuse the views." So Ra'avad, peace be upon him, took issue with him for saying that one who says that God is a body is a sectarian. And it is not fitting to think that Ra'avad's view, peace be upon him, is that he is not a sectarian — for surely one who corporealizes God is a sectarian. Rather, their dispute hangs on this: that Rambam, according to the apparent sense of his language, holds that one who says that God is corporeal is a sectarian, even though this error stems from his not being habituated in divine matters, and from his having chased after the plain senses of the Scriptures and the midrashim, not descending into their depth to understand their matters as they truly are. And to this Ra'avad objected, of blessed memory, and contradicted him, and said that such a man — who in all his affairs serves God and walks in the ways of the Torah in innocence, and who, through the shortness of his knowledge, believed in corporeality — is not called a sectarian, though he certainly errs, since his intent is not to do evil, God forbid. But one who recognizes his Creator, to whom the gates of the premises in the removal of corporeality have been revealed, and who does not acknowledge the truth, but is brazen and says that God is a body — this one is surely called a sectarian, even according to the view of Ra'avad, of blessed memory. And likewise we say regarding the matter of the Sefirot: that surely one who did not know of them and believed in the simple One without knowledge of the Sefirot ought not to be called a heretic [kofer], God forbid, nor "one who cuts among the saplings" [mekatzetz ba-neti'ot], God forbid. For if so, it would have been fitting that, when a person is able to understand the training in the commandments, they should train him in the matter of belief in the Sefirot and the knowledge of them — which we do not find to be so. But on the contrary, they said that it is fitting to conceal them, and that these matters are transmitted only to the modest, etc. This is not so with the matter of the existence of God, and the unity, and the matter of Torah from Heaven, and the prophecy of Moses, and most of the principles of the religion: for when the lad knows how to call "my father" and "my mother," they train him in them and reveal to him the plain sense of the matters, as our Sages of blessed memory said in Tractate Sukkah (42a): once he knows how to speak, his father teaches him Torah and the Shema. And they asked in the Gemara, "What is 'Torah'?" and they said, "'Moses commanded us the Torah,' etc."; and "the Shema" is "Hear, O Israel," etc.

Now, they chose these two verses because in them are included most of the corners of the cardinal principles of the Torah. In the verse "Hear, O Israel" is included the existence of God — namely, "YHVH." Further, that He exercises providence, and even particular providence — and this is the meaning of "Eloheinu (our God)." For although His existence is necessary in respect of the whole world entire — and He was, is, and will be, and brings into being all the existents (which is the meaning of the four-letter Name in its writing); and although He is Master of all worlds, upper and lower (which is the meaning of its reading in lordship [Adonut]) — and from this His providence is necessitated as encompassing the whole world: even so, "Eloheinu" means that He watches over us in particular. "YHVH is One (echad)" necessitates the unity. And they have already explained in the Gemara (Berakhot 13b) that a person must intend, in the word echad, that He is King above and below and in the four directions. And by this it is necessitated that He is not a body, for the corporeal cannot be found in differing places at one time. Further, the meaning of echad: [it means] not like one of an enumeration, etc., as we shall explain in the Gate of Self and Vessels, in Gate 4, ch.5, with the help of God. And in the verse "Moses commanded us the Torah" is included the cardinal principle of Torah from Heaven, and prophecy, and the prophecy of Moses — and this is "Moses commanded us the Torah," as is well known. Reward and punishment — in his saying "an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob," for YHVH desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to make Israel meritorious and to bequeath them His Torah. And this is what they intended in saying these two verses: for the reason that, when the lad grows, he begins to roam in his thought among these words, and asks his father and his elder their reason and their matter; and they tell it to him and bring him into the matters of the corners of the Torah little by little, according to his understanding, as he is able to bear. This is what is found regarding the existence of the cardinal principles. Not so with the supernal Sefirot — on the contrary, they conceal their secret from every eye, and reveal them only to the modest, the unique ones in the generation. And here, then, is proof that one who does not discern the matter of the Sefirot is not, on this account, called a heretic [kofer], nor "one who cuts among the saplings," God forbid. Rather, what we may rightly say of him is that he did not merit to behold the luminaries in his days, nor tasted the sweetness of the Torah and the nectar of its pleasant sayings; and behold, he died without wisdom and saw no good. The second way: these are those to whom the matter of the Sefirot and their existence were revealed, and who deny them because of the evil of their disposition — for they were habituated in external sciences, and "with the children of strangers they content themselves." And these, even if they not be called heretics (koferim) or sectarians (minim), inasmuch as they believe in all the matters of divinity — even so they are called heretics (koferim), because they deny an interpretation of the Oral Torah. And one of the three [kinds of] heretics is one who denies an interpretation among the interpretations of the Oral Torah, as Rambam wrote in the aforementioned chapter; and he also denies the words of our Sages of blessed memory. And besides what is already his, he adds to his sin a transgression: for from the denial of the Sefirot, heresy will follow — for we will compel him by the premises and corners of the Torah: since the simple One is not subject to change, how does He watch over passing matters? And likewise, since He is one, how does He watch over the kinds of species — for that would necessitate multiplicity, as is known? And therefore he is compelled to believe in the Sefirot; and if not, he falls into heresy, God forbid — as many have erred in [the matter of] the removal of particular providence, and in these matters, which it is not fitting to raise up in writing.

And so, perforce we compel him to belief in the Sefirot, or he is called a heretic. And by this path it is necessitated that one who says he has no dealing with Kabbalah, and does not wish to direct his prayer except to the Master of the lights — as many have thought — surely is called one who errs. For if a person comes to speak of the simple One in respect of its aspect toward its [own] existence, apart from its existence and its aspect in respect of the Sefirot, he is found to remove its actions altogether. For the Ein Sof, in respect of the aspect of its Self, is simple and is not a possessor of changes — that it should change from judgment to mercy, and be moved by will, and change from will to will through prayer — except in respect of its aspect toward its Sefirot, which are its [acts of] providence, and through which the change of judgment and mercy occurs. And let the inquirer not press to enter, by means of these our words, within the partition, to understand the matter of the changes and the providence — for harm will reach him, and not benefit; rather, we shall explain the matter at length in the Gate of Self and Vessels, with God's help. In sum: a person is compelled to believe in the Sefirot in order to be correct in the cardinal principles of the faith and in its corners, which cannot be upheld except through them — that is, by means of them — for through them the Emanator effects the changes, and from this no change whatsoever reaches Him, God forbid, as is explained at length in that lovely Gate. And of God we ask forgiveness.

After we have occupied ourselves with the matter of the Sefirot, and the necessity of their existence, and the matter transmitted concerning them among the sages, we need to know their essence and their names — the comprehensive [naming] agreed upon among the commentators, and in particular in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him. And this is it: the first, Keter; the second, Chokhmah; the third, Binah; the fourth, Gedulah or Chesed; the fifth, Pachad or Gevurah; the sixth, Tiferet; the seventh, Netzach; the eighth, Hod; the ninth, Yesod; the tenth, Malkhut. And these Sefirot are ten Names that may not be erased; and the Names and the Sefirot are all one thing, for the spirituality of the Names is the very Sefirot. Keter is Ehyeh, and it is not found in Scripture except three times in one verse (Exodus 3:14): "And God said to Moses, Ehyeh asher Ehyeh (I will be what I will be); and He said, Thus shall you say to the children of Israel, Ehyeh has sent me to you." But the reason it does not appear [more] in the Torah, and other doubts in this inquiry, will be explained in the Gate of the Names, with the help of God. And the Name of Chokhmah is Yah, and there are many of these written: in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "My strength and song is Yah," and "For a hand is upon the throne of Yah." Repeated in the Prophets: "I shall not see Yah, Yah, in the land of the living," which is in the writing of Hezekiah. Tripled in the Writings: "From the straits I called Yah; Yah answered me with expansiveness," and many like them. And the Name of Binah is the four-letter Name with the vocalization of Elohim, written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "Adonai YHVH, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it," and many like it. Repeated in the Prophets: "YHVH Adonai is my strength, and He makes my feet [like hinds']," etc., and many like it. Tripled in the Writings: "I will come in the mighty acts of Adonai YHVH; I will make mention of Your righteousness, Yours alone," and many like it. And the Name of Chesed is the Name El, and there are many of these in the Torah, in the Prophets, and in the Writings. In the Torah: "And he called it El, God of Israel," and many like it. In the Prophets: "El, Elohim, YHVH — He knows," etc., and many like it. In the Writings: "El, whose way is perfect," and many like it. And the Name of Gevurah is Elohim, written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "And Elohim tested Abraham," and many like it. Repeated in the Prophets: "And there was a terror of Elohim," and many like it. Tripled in the Writings: "Arise, O Elohim, judge the earth," and many like it. And the Name of Tiferet is YHVH — written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "And YHVH said," "And YHVH spoke," and many others. Repeated in the Prophets: "Thus said YHVH," and many others. Tripled in the Writings: "YHVH said to me, You are My son," and many like it. And the Name of Netzach you will not find alone, but only joined with the Name of Hod — for the reason that the two of them have one Name, which is Tzeva'ot. And this is not found in the Torah at all; but in the Prophets, many: "Thus said YHVH Tzeva'ot," and many others. And as for the Name of Yesod, all the later commentators explained that its proper Name is El Chai. But this is difficult, for El Chai is not among the Names that may not be erased — for the word Chai is not holy, as it appears in Tractate Shevuot (35a), where they counted there only [the Name] El. And the Name El, which is the holy one, is borrowed for it from Chesed by way of the epithets, and they counted it. And among those holding this view is Rabbi Abba in the book of the Zohar, Parashat Vayikra (11a), and these are his words: "The sixth and the seventh are called Tzeva'ot. The eighth is El Chai, as it is said, 'For there YHVH commanded the blessing — life,' etc.; and this is the Tzaddik, from whom all life issues."

And as for his having counted Netzach and Hod as sixth and seventh — although they are seventh and eighth, as is known — it is because Rabbi Abba began to count the Names from the Name Yah, from Chokhmah, as is explained there. And he explained that the Tzaddik is called El Chai for the reason that the issuing-place of life is from him; and he said "from whom all life issues," because the root of life is above, in Chokhmah and Binah, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:12), "wisdom gives life to its possessors," and as we shall explain in the Gate of the Values of the Allusions, with the help of God. For this [reason] he said that the reason Yesod is called by the Name El Chai — although the root of life is above — is because he is their source in respect of their issuing forth; and on that account he adopted the expression "issue" (nafkin), that is, in respect of issuing.

Behold, then, that Rabbi Abba explained that the Name of Yesod is El Chai. And Rabbi Elazar (there, 11b) disputed him and said that its Name is Shaddai, and these are his words: "The ninth is Shaddai, for He said to the world, 'Enough (dai)' — for 'dai' is sufficiency; and sufficiency comes to the world only from the Tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world (yesod olam), who said to the world, 'Enough.'"

And because it was difficult for Rabbi Elazar that the Name Shaddai means "He said to the world, Enough" — that is, that He set it a limit, in that its boundaries were stretching ever onward until He said to it, "Enough" — and this cannot rightly apply to Yesod, since the creation of the world was by way of the Architect, which is Malkhut, and so it is surely she who said to the world, "Enough" — therefore he said that Shaddai means sufficiency and sustenance, and the sustenance is from the side of Yesod, and it is he who supplies sustenance to the world; and this is "and sufficiency comes to the world only from the Tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world." And he intended to say [the acrostic] Tzaddik-Yesod-Olam, for he is the foundation that establishes the world; and this is why he doubled his expression and said, "the Tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world, who said to the world, 'Enough.'" Even so, we do not deny that the Name El Chai is in Yesod, as Rabbi Abba explained — but not that it is a holy Name in the manner of the other Names that may not be erased, but rather an epithet like the other epithets; and it comes in Scripture (Psalms 84:3): "my heart and my flesh sing out to El, the living God (El Chai)." And the Name Shaddai is written in the Torah: "And El Shaddai will bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you"; repeated in the Prophets: "like the voice of Shaddai when they went"; tripled in the Writings: "and Shaddai will be your defense." And the Name of Malkhut is Adonai, written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "And now, let the power of Adonai be magnified," and many like it; repeated in the Prophets: "A word has the Adonai sent against Jacob," and many like it; tripled in the Writings: "Adonai, open my lips," and many like it. And it has come in the Masorah that there are 134 of them in Scripture; and the reason for this you will find in Chizkuni's commentary on the Torah, at its beginning, where he said that this number corresponds to the letters of the initial and final letters of the words mizrach (east), ma'arav (west), darom (south) — to say that these three directions are shut up in the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He; and likewise [the number] 134 (k-l-d) is a term of shutting, like aklidei (keys); but north is not included, for it is open, to exact [punishment] from the wicked, and in the time to come the Holy One, blessed be He, will shut it up as well, etc. — see there, and you will find reasons that follow from this inquiry. And these ten aforementioned Names are palaces (heikhalot) for the spirituality of the Sefirot; and that spirituality is a garment for their inner spirituality, alluded to in the four-letter Name within each and every Sefirah. And this matter, and others besides it, in the explanation of these Names and the matters of the Sefirot, will be explained in the coming Gates, with the help of God, each and every one in its fitting place.
And so this Gate is concluded; and thanks be to God, who has helped us — may He help us — forever, Selah, and ever. Amen.
The Second Gate is the Gate of the Reason for the Emanation:

On the reason why ten and not more. After we occupied ourselves in the preceding Gate with the necessity of the Emanation, and with its being agreed among the Kabbalists that they are ten, no fewer and no more, and set out their matter and their names, we have seen fit in this Gate to give a reason for their being ten, and for the matter of the Emanation as a whole, in general, with the help of God.
Chapter One:

As we were taking our delight in the garden of delights that is the books of the sages of this wisdom, we found that the sage Rabbi Yehudah Chayyat, in his book Minchat Yehudah (fol. 9b), wrote, on the reason for the ten, one reason in the name of Rabbi Azriel, with its rebuttal beside it. And these are his words: "Know that every point comes with three diameters [kotarim] — length, breadth and depth — and when you multiply them by one another, in the manner of a square number, the three make nine; and with the place that bears them they are ten." Thus far the words of Rabbi Azriel, of blessed memory. And Rabbi Yehudah objected to him, and these are his words: "This reason does not seem good to me, on two grounds. The first: the premise is not true, because the diameters mentioned have quantity, and the point has no quantity, for it is the end of the line. And further: would it be good in the eyes of YHVH that the diameters mentioned, by which body is defined, be attributed to the Emanation? For in divinity, body [geshem, which also means 'rain'] 'is over and gone.'" Thus far [his] words.

And because his words are somewhat obscure — particularly in the first difficulty, where he says "the point has no quantity," etc. — we have seen fit to explain his intent. The matter is this: every corporeal thing has length, breadth and depth, and there is no corporeal thing in the world that lacks these three, for they are the dimensions of body [gidrei ha-guf, 'what defines a body']. Were one to conceive of two of the dimensions of body alone, namely length and breadth without depth, it would be called a plane [shetach], meaning something like color spread [shatuach] over the face of paper, of which length and breadth can properly be said, but not depth; and therefore it is called a plane. And when we conceive of one dimension of body alone, namely length without breadth, it is called a line [kav], meaning a line of length, stripped of breadth and all the more of depth. And when we conceive of the negation of all three dimensions of body, that thing is called a point [nekudah]: that is, it has neither length nor breadth nor depth. And this is not because it could be so in reality; rather, it is called a notional point [nekudah tzurit] — that is, the notion [tziyur] of the negation of the dimensions of body, and not that it exists in reality. With this premise the intent of Rabbi Yehudah will be understood, in objecting to Rabbi Azriel that his words contradict themselves: for he said "a point comes with three diameters," and this is impossible, since a point has neither length nor breadth nor depth, but is "the end of the line" — meaning, as we have explained, that it is the end of the line, which is likewise the negation of length; so the point turns out to have no diameters at all. And his statement that it is the end of the line is not agreed among the masters of astronomy [ba'alei ha-tekhunah]. For some say that two points or more, gathered together, make a line; and some say that even if all the points in the world were gathered, they would not make a line: since the point has no length at all, it is impossible that length should come to be through it. But this is not our principal concern.

Now Rabbi Yehudah resolved his two objections to the view of Rabbi Azriel by way of number, in Rabbi Azriel's defense; but since the thing is neither seemly nor acceptable, we shall not copy it here. It seems right to us to argue in Rabbi Azriel's favor, and to say: it is true that the Emanation is neither body nor corporeality. Nevertheless, body and corporeality proceed from it. And just as the masters of the Kabbalah held that the four elements — water, fire, air and earth — are alluded to in the Sefirot (Gedulah being the element of water, Gevurah the element of fire, Tiferet the element of air, and Malkhut the element of earth), not because these are literally elements, God forbid, but because they are the root of the elements, and the elements are created from their root: so it is with the dimensions of body. The point is not that there is literally body above, nor that the dimensions of body can properly be said of the Sefirot; rather, since body is created from them and they are its root, the dimensions of body are found in the roots by way of allusion [kinnui]. Therefore we may properly speak, above, of "length, breadth and depth," meaning the power by which length is made, the power by which breadth is made, and the power by which depth is made. And likewise each of these three powers performs three further actions, so that they turn out to be nine; and that which brings the existence of body into being, before it comes into its dimensions, is a tenth power. Thus ten powers are necessary above, and these are the ten Sefirot. And it is not that Rabbi Azriel's view is that the dimensions of body exist above, Heaven forbid. Further, it seems that the difficulty was none at all to begin with, for Rabbi Azriel did well in likening the Emanation to the dimensions of body, since permission for this has already been given.

And indeed Sefer Yetzirah took this very path in saying "depth of height and depth of below, and height and below, and east and west, and south and north" — these are the dimensions of body; and yet Sefer Yetzirah did not refrain from applying the likeness to divinity, since they are a parable and a likeness for the subject under discussion. And as for the second difficulty, that the point has no quantity: this is no objection. For there is certainly no point that does not have dimensions; and if we said above that the point has no quantity, that is only the notional point, which does not exist in reality, whereas a point that exists in reality has diameters. If so, this is no objection.
And further: because the Emanation is not body or corporeality, he referred to it by the term "point," which is not a body — since the Emanation is the root of body and of its dimensions.

And further, he referred to the Emanation by the term "point" to say that, just as the point is unified in its parts and admits of no parts at all, so the Emanation admits of no parts; and even if we speak of parts in it, it is all parable and likeness. Thus far what has seemed right to us to argue in favor of Rabbi Azriel. And now we shall write what Rabbi Yehudah wrote on the reason for the Emanation, and these are his words: "Since the Emanation comes in a point, we must perforce acknowledge that this point has a beginning, a middle and an end [rosh, tokh, sof]. We must acknowledge an end, since we see that, had [things] been created from the side of the power that has no end, they would go on without end and would exist forever; and that was not the intention. And since it has an end, it therefore has a beginning, for there is no end without a beginning and no beginning without an end. But beware of thinking, when I say 'beginning, middle and end,' that a beginning, middle and end in quantity are meant, Heaven forbid; rather, [they are meant] in respect of power, for there is a difference between the cause and the effect. And since each of the three extremities mentioned in the point is composed of the three — for in the beginning there are end and middle, and so in the middle, and so in the end — they come to nine, when we multiply three by three in the manner of a square number; and the place that bears [them], etc." Thus far [his] words.

These are some of his words, in brief; and he brought many passages from the Zohar as proof. But since the passages are no proof at all for his words, we have not seen fit to copy them. And the difficulty that should be raised, whether against his words or against the words of Rabbi Azriel, peace be upon him, is this: since the reason for the ten is the point, which has three, each composed of three — then we too may say that each part of the three in each of the three parts is itself composed of the three, and so they mount up without end, from three to three. And if we do not wish to include them [in one another] in this way, then the first inclusion, by which we make three into nine — whence do we have it? This is certainly very forced: so much so that, on account of it, there are those who wished to combine the two views, and said that every point has depth, length and breadth, and each of these three has an end, a middle and a beginning [sof, tokh, rosh], making nine, and the place that bears them makes ten. And I am able to object to the holders of these three views, for I see no place for these things: since it turns out that bodies and limit are what necessitate the existence of the Emanation. And it is not acceptable to say that, because these are necessary dimensions, the Sefirot were compelled to be of this measure; for it is the Sefirot that acted and begot the world and all created beings. Indeed, if the Sefirot were sixteen, the dimensions could exist as sixteen things, four by four. Who ever saw fit to make the bringing-about of the form of the father necessary on account of the existence of the form of the son? Would you say that Reuben had to have hands so that his son should have hands — or, again, that Reuben must have three hands so that his son should have three hands? How can we make the form of the cause necessary on account of the form of the effect? For in truth the cause is the principal thing and the effect is secondary to it; and how can the effect be what necessitates the form of its cause's existence? I wonder at this.

And further, as to the words of Rabbi Yehudah, who said that the point has an end, a middle and a beginning, and that each of the three has an end, a middle and a beginning: this too does not come out well. For a middle cannot have an end and a beginning: if it had an end and a beginning it would not be a middle; and of that which is a middle, "end" and "beginning" cannot properly be said, since its beginning is the first beginning and its end is the last end. For "end" and "beginning" here are not a quantitative end and beginning, but the cessation of the power, or its beginning. And how can one say that there is a power that has a cessation of its power, or a beginning of it, other than its final cessation or its first beginning — that is, its very own beginning and end?

And further: since "beginning" and "end" mean nothing but the cessation of the power or its beginning, as has been explained, then, since the end is the cessation of the power, how can we speak, in that cessation, of a beginning and a middle? For it is nothing but cessation — the power has ceased — and in cessation there is no beginning and no middle. (Though some of this can be resolved, with strain.) And as with the difficulty he himself raised against Rabbi Azriel — how can the diameters of the corporeal be attributed to the Emanation, "for in divinity," etc. — is it any easier on his own view? How can cessation of power and beginning of power occur in the Emanation? For of divinity no lack of power can properly be said, God forbid, for it is perfect with the utmost perfection. Perforce we must answer this in one of two ways. The first: it is necessary because there is a difference between the Ein Sof and the emanated, like the difference between cause and effect; and so some cessation of power can properly be said of it, since it is necessarily not exactly like the Emanator, having descended from Him and being emanated from Him. And this is no deficiency in the Emanator, God forbid, nor in the emanated; rather, because it is emanated and an effect, it must descend a grade from its cause. This is due to the superiority of the Emanator over the emanated, and for this reason cessation of power can properly be said of it, in a certain respect. Or we may say that there had to be a limit in their action, in order to fulfil the intent of the Emanator, which was that created beings should be finite and subject to cessation. If so, then according to the words of Rabbi Azriel too we may say that limit was necessary in the Emanation, for these reasons. First: because the First Cause is the utmost negation of cessation, both in notion and in quantity, altogether; whereas those emanated from Him are necessarily limited somewhat, in the measure of their descent from before Him, by a notional limit and not an actual limit. Yet relative to the Emanator, who is their cause, from whom we are obliged to negate limit and cessation and all such things, the emanated must have a difference from Him, like the difference of the effect from the cause.

And further, second: so that the created beings that proceed from the emanated should be limited. And this is His power, blessed be He: for just as the world was created Something from Nothing [yesh me-ayin], so the Ein Sof, King of kings of kings, emanated the emanated, from whom there would proceed finite actions, so that created beings would be limited. And the inquirer into this must bring his mind to understand, and establish it and support it and direct it toward the truth. Let him not think that our intent in this is to set a limit either to the Emanator or to the emanated, Heaven forbid and forfend. Rather, the intent is this: after we have negated body and limit and quantity and cessation of power and finitude and end from the pure and holy Emanation, with the utmost negation and distancing, we are obliged by absolute necessity to rise yet higher, to a more exalted and more choice grade, in the case of the Ein Sof, the Emanator, King of kings of kings. And that is why they called Him Ein Sof ['without end'], for the reason mentioned. And few words on this matter are good and seemly; of this and the like it is said (Proverbs 27:26), "Lambs [kevasim] are for your clothing" [which the Sages read: things that are the hidden matters (kivshono) of the world should be kept under your clothing]. Nevertheless, we have seen fit to prove the matter conclusively from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 70, fol. 130a), and these are his words: "The supernal Keter, although it is a primordial light, a clear light, a refined light, is dark before the Cause of Causes." Thus far [his] words.

The meaning is: although it is a clear light, etc. — the utmost of purity, and without limit, and we are obliged to negate density and limit from it — nevertheless we are obliged to believe that it has density and limit, and a cessation of light and of power, relative to the Emanator who is its cause. And that is why he here referred to the Ein Sof by the expression "Cause of Causes": the intent is to establish the matter by absolute necessity, for He is the cause of all the causes, and therefore He must necessarily have a rank above them all. For if we were to strip the Emanation of every deficiency whatever and raise it to the most perfect grade possible, a denial of the existence of a First Cause would follow: since Keter would be at a rank than which there is no higher, what then would be the rank by which the Emanator rises above it? Therefore we are obliged to leave room in which to raise the Emanator above all the emanated, even while we raise the emanated as far as is possible. And this is a thing a person must contemplate; let him not be hasty to reply.

Rabbi Yehudah wrote yet another reason, and wrote that it is more satisfactory than the reason of Rabbi Azriel that we copied in the preceding chapter; and these are his words: "The all-inclusive number is ten, and there is none besides it. For everything above ten returns to the units — whether on the side of the units, like eleven, twelve, thirteen, or on the side of the tens, like twenty, thirty, forty, which are multiples in the series of the tens. And since the Emanation enters into number, it is fitting that it should take the most inclusive number there is." Thus far [his] words.

As for his saying "since the Emanation enters into number": the meaning is that they had to have number so that created beings should have number and limit, as we explained above. But the difficulty that can be raised is this: what causes the all-inclusive number to be ten and not twenty, or a hundred, so that the return of the ranks does not begin [only] from twenty upward? We would answer that the cause of this is that the Sefirot are ten; for if the Sefirot were twenty, the number too would run to twenty. And this is certainly true; and it is a more satisfactory and more acceptable account that the Sefirot be the principal thing and number secondary — and not the reverse, that number should be ten for no reason, and that this should be the cause of the Emanation's being of that number.

And further: the Sefirot are a cause prior to all created beings, and they are the causes of all that is from them and below. How, then, can number, which is posterior, be the cause of the Sefirot, which are prior? This is certainly very forced. Yet although we reject these answers as the reason for the Emanation, we do not deny that it is true that number and the Emanation have a relation and a great affinity. For number is ten, and it rises from ten to ten without end, and never rises beyond ten; and so it is with the Sefirot.

And further: numbers are ten, and from ten they rise to a hundred, and from a hundred they rise to a thousand — and that is elef ['thousand'], which is one [alef], in the secret of the return of the matter to complete unity. So it is with the Sefirot, in all of which [all are included]: for ten times ten is a hundred, and when we include them once again they are a thousand, that is, alef, in the secret of pele ['wonder'], which is the return of things to their source, in the secret of the unity. And there are several other great principles that depend on number, which are principles of the Torah, as we shall write in the Gate of Combination, with the help of God. And we cannot think of anything in the world that resembles the Emanation more than number does. Likewise we do not deny that it is true that the Emanation is three [sets] of three each, and an all-inclusive power: that is, three, which are Chesed [lovingkindness], Din [judgment] and Rachamim [mercy], with three in each of them. In Chesed there are an end, a middle and a beginning [sof, tokh, rosh]: namely Chokhmah the beginning, Chesed the middle and Netzach the end. Likewise in Din: the beginning is Binah, the middle Gevurah and the end Hod. And likewise in Rachamim: Tiferet the beginning, Yesod the middle and Malkhut the end. And the supernal Keter includes them all, as we shall explain at greater length in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter twenty-five, with God's help. And this matter is deep, as we shall set out at length there. But for all that, we shall hold truthfully to what is true: that these things do not suffice at all as a reason for the Emanation, as explained above. Rabbi Menachem Recanati, of blessed memory, wrote yet another reason, for the seven Sefirot of the Structure [binyan], one by one, in his book Ta'amei ha-Mitzvot [the Reasons for the Commandments], in the discussion of the Self and the vessels; and Rabbi Yehudah Chayyat, of blessed memory, copied his words: "And now we shall explain how the world needs these seven extremities, which are Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod and Malkhut. The beginning of the Structure is Chesed, for there can be no structure without it: that is, by this attribute the Holy One, blessed be He, whitens the iniquities of Israel. And in Sefer Yetzirah this attribute is called 'she who whitens the iniquities of Israel'; and she pardons them for what is done from the side of Gevurah, for the evil inclination flows from there. And this Sefirah is emanated from Binah, which is above it. But the first three are intellective and are not called attributes, and we are not at present engaged in explaining them. And this is a great lovingkindness [chesed] that the Holy One, blessed be He, does with His creatures: that He passes over [their iniquities] one by one, the first each time, and is reconciled to them, even though strict justice does not warrant it. Therefore the world cannot endure without this pillar. And in Sefer ha-Bahir I found this: The attribute of Chesed said, 'All the days that Abraham was in the world I did not need to do my work, for Abraham stood there in my place and kept my charge. For this is my work: I acquit the world, even when they have been found liable.

"'And further, I turn them back and put it into their hearts to do the will of their Father in heaven. All this Abraham did.' Further, the world needs the second pillar, which is Din [judgment], the opposite of the first attribute we mentioned. Were it not for this pillar, punishment would not reach the wicked, and every man would rob and kill his fellow with none to exact payment from him. Therefore the world needs to be governed by this pillar, so that payment may be exacted from the wicked. And this Sefirah was emanated from the Chesed we mentioned, and it is called 'fire from water,' meaning fire that came out of water; and as water is the opposite of fire, so the actions of this attribute are the opposite of the action of the other attribute. And these two are called 'the arms of the world,' as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:27), 'and beneath are the arms of the world.' Further, the world needs a third pillar, which is Tiferet. It is the intermediate attribute; it receives from both of them and stands between the two. And the world's need for this attribute is because the first two attributes are not enough for the world. For if one who has become liable were judged by the second attribute, which is the attribute of judgment, it would judge him without compassion, being the attribute of harsh judgment, and it would likewise [punish] the meritorious and the good, above, altogether. And if he were judged by the attribute of Chesed, even his few iniquities would not be remembered against him, even in this world. Therefore the world needs the intermediate attribute, like a person who joins two things together and unites them in a single subject, in order 'to give to each man according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds': so that if the righteous have sinned, payment is exacted from them in this world, and if the wicked have performed commandments, their good reward is paid to them in this world. And this attribute is called 'east,' for from there light went out to the world; and the sphere of the sun corresponds to it, for the attribute of day flows from it. Further, the world needs a fourth pillar and a fifth pillar, which are Netzach and Hod. They flow and are emanated from the Gedulah and the Gevurah that we mentioned above, as it is said (Psalms 16:11), 'pleasantness at Your right hand, Netzach' — meaning that Netzach is on the right, set directly beneath Chesed, and Hod on the left, set directly beneath Gevurah.

"And Netzach has the sense of victory [nitzuach]: that is, by this attribute lovingkindness and merit are victorious over the accusers. And for this one must give thanks to YHVH, and this is Hod, in the sense of thanksgiving [hoda'ah] to the Name, who founded this pillar; for without the help of YHVH a person could not stand before the Satan. Further, the world needs a sixth pillar and a seventh pillar, which are Yesod and Malkhut; they are the likeness of male and female, and all flows into Malkhut, which is called Shekhinah and the Assembly of Israel [Knesset Yisrael], for all the Sefirot dwell [shokhenot] in her; and we have already explained this above. And therefore our Sages, of blessed memory, called her 'bride' [kallah], and in the Song of Songs too she is called 'bride,' because she is composed [kelulah] of all. And she is in the west [ma'arav], as our Sages, of blessed memory, said, 'the Shekhinah is in the west,' because there all is mingled [mit'arev]." Thus far [his] words on the reason for the Emanation. And although it is true that most of what he says is right, nevertheless these things do not suffice as a reason for the Emanation. For once judgment and punishment, lovingkindness and reward, are found in the two attributes Chesed and Gevurah, and the intermediate attribute is Tiferet, what further need is there for the other Sefirot? Why should the victory over the accuser and the evil inclination not lie in Gevurah — as in truth it does? For so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained: that a person's prevailing [gover] over his inclination is from the side of Gevurah; and we shall treat this at length in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter three. Likewise thanksgiving, on his account, is not an attribute that acts, but only that a person should give thanks to the Name; and was it necessary to emanate a Sefirah just for the thanks that a person owes to YHVH? I wonder at this. Further, why Yesod and Malkhut? Since Chesed and Din come together in the intermediate [attribute] and are united, what need is there of male and female at all, for the sake of mingling? For the powers have already been mingled in the intermediate [attribute].
And further: in this manner we cannot give a reason for the first three at all, as he said explicitly.

And further — God forbid — is the hand of the Emanator too short to emanate one emanation only, that is, a single Sefirah in which there would be the power of punishment, of reward and of the intermediate? And there is no rebuttal from the wording of the Mishnah (Avot 5:1), "By ten utterances the world was created. And could it not have been created by one utterance?" etc. For, on the contrary, the Mishnah means the opposite of what he said: that although the world was created through differing things that indicate judgment, mercy and the intermediate, it could nevertheless have been created by the power of a single utterance, that is, a single Sefirah. This shows that it is not beyond His power for the power of all ten to be in the power of a single Sefirah. That is the meaning of "And could it not have been created by one utterance," etc.: it is certainly speaking of the creation of the world as it now is. And as for its saying "but rather to exact payment": the meaning is not as Rabbi Menachem supposed. Rather, it concerns finitude — or [what proceeds] from that which is not finite — or something else, as we shall explain at length in the coming chapters, with the help of God. Therefore this reason does not at all satisfy our desire or quench our thirst.

After we have written, in the preceding chapters, all the reasons that the commentators wrote, whether many or few, and have raised our points against them as Heaven has shown us, we have resolved to speak on this matter as it falls to our lot. And before anything else we say: "I see the men, but the objection I do not see." For this question must take one of two paths. Either the question of the reason for the ten is put to us — that is, whence do we have proof, from the Torah or from investigation, for our tradition; or the question is put to the Emanator, the Ein Sof, King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He: why did He emanate ten and not some other number? And we shall speak to each of these. If the question is put to us — that is, whence do we have support for the tradition that they are ten, so that we should not say they are twenty, or five, or one — it is no question to begin with. For we have proof upon proof in the Torah of Moses, which reveals these hidden secrets to us and enlightens our eyes in them: in the creation of the world by ten utterances; in the giving of the Torah by ten Commandments; and King David, peace be upon him, in the ten kinds of praise in the psalm "Praise El in His sanctuary," with which he sealed his book. And this matter has already been explained in tractate Rosh Hashanah (fol. 32), for we read there: "These ten Kingships [Malkhuyot] — to what do they correspond? Rabbi said: to the ten praises that David spoke in the book of Psalms. — But there are many praises! — Those of which it is written, 'Praise Him with the blast of the shofar.' Rav Yosef said: to the Ten Commandments that were spoken to Moses at Sinai. Rabbi Yochanan said: to the ten utterances by which the world was created. — Which are they? The 'And He said' of Genesis. — But those are nine! — 'In the beginning' is also an utterance, as it is written, 'By the word of YHVH the heavens were made.'" Thus far [its] words.
In truth this passage is, on the face of it, difficult as regards Rabbi Yochanan, who answered, "'In the beginning' is also an utterance."

For "In the beginning" alludes to Chokhmah, which is called "beginning" [reshit], and the large bet alludes to it. If so, even though "In the beginning" is also an utterance, there are still [only] nine; and this is the difficulty. For then what was troubling the questioner? If his difficulty was that Chokhmah is not in the count, there would be eight, and that is the objection he should have raised. And if his difficulty was that Keter is not in the count, then why was he satisfied when he was answered "'In the beginning' [is also an utterance]," etc.? He should have objected: even though "In the beginning" is also an utterance, still, with "In the beginning" there are nine, for "In the beginning" is Chokhmah. This is a general question about the utterances mentioned in this passage. And likewise, from this difficulty one could prove the view of Rabbi Shem Tov ben Shem Tov, author of Sefer ha-Emunot, whose words we shall copy in the Gate of Whether the Ein Sof is the Keter, chapter three. This is the Da'at view: he holds that Keter is not in the count of the Sefirot, but that the ten Sefirot run from Chokhmah downward; and since the count pressed him, he said that a further Sefirah was newly added to it, called Da'at, which is below Chokhmah and Binah and above Chesed and Gevurah. We shall treat the matter at length there. Now on his account it turns out that the utterances begin only from Chokhmah, and even so there are nine without "In the beginning," which is Chokhmah, and ten with "In the beginning," which is Chokhmah. And because of the ruin that would follow from this passage, before we raise further points about it or explain anything in it at all, it is fitting that we look to setting this matter right. And we say that this [view] is impossible. For since Rabbi Shem Tov admitted with his own mouth that Da'at is what is mentioned in the verse (Proverbs 3:20), "By His knowledge [da'at] the depths were split," and likewise in what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Chagigah fol. 12; and there it reads "by ten things the world was created," three of them being wisdom, etc.), "by three things the world was created: by wisdom [chokhmah], by understanding [tevunah] and by knowledge [da'at]" — it is compelled by the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that [this] Da'at is the mode of existence of Tiferet that is concealed between Abba and Imma [Father and Mother]; and this is what is called BeN-YaH ['son of Yah'], through which Chokhmah and Binah are united, as we shall explain these matters at length in that Gate.

Accordingly, we should ask: what distinguishes this Da'at — which is the concealed mode of existence of Tiferet, emanated between Abba and Imma — that it should effect an utterance of its own, from the other modes of existence of the Sefirot, which did not effect utterances, although their coming-into-being preceded the coming-into-being of this Da'at? Take the mode of existence of Binah concealed within Chokhmah: just as Chokhmah itself acted, the concealed Binah ought also to act. Likewise the mode of existence of Gevurah concealed within Binah, and the mode of existence of Chesed concealed within Chokhmah: each of them ought to have effected one utterance, besides the utterance that belongs to it in its revealed mode of existence, as with Da'at and Tiferet. Nor can it be said that the reason Da'at effected an utterance of its own is that Da'at is the mode of existence of Tiferet with its mate at its side — they being the mode of existence of "the two great luminaries" — and that because they were united the two together effected one utterance, like the other Sefirot, whereas after the moon made her accusation and was diminished and driven out, the luminaries were divided in two, and Tiferet went back and effected an utterance of its own, and Malkhut an utterance of her own. For if so, why did Tiferet not effect an utterance of its own from the outset, and Malkhut one of her own, even while they were united in the utmost union? For it cannot be denied that they were two Sefirot. Otherwise — if they are counted as only one Sefirah — it turns out that before the diminishment the Sefirot were nine and not ten, since Malkhut and Tiferet are one Sefirah; and likewise, when she returns to her first place, they will be nine. And this is impossible by the law of this wisdom, as explained in the preceding Gate.

And further: the ten Commandments and the ten utterances are one matter, as is evident from the passage we copied above. And so it is evident in the Zohar, Parashat Yitro (fol. 93b), and these are its words: "These ten sayings of the Torah are the sum of all the commandments of the Torah, the sum of above and below, the sum of all the ten sayings of 'In the beginning.'" Thus far [its] words.

It said "the sum of all the commandments of the Torah" because Rashbi, peace be upon him, holds that the six hundred and thirteen commandments are included in the ten Commandments, as is explained in Parashat Yitro, and likewise included in the ten utterances, as is evident in Parashat Bereshit and in the Tikkunim. That is why it said that the ten Commandments are the sum of the commandments. And it likewise said that they are the sum of the ten utterances: meaning that whatever is made clear from the ten utterances of the account of Creation is made clear from the ten Commandments of the giving of the Torah, to the eyes of the discerning. Now we say: since the ten Commandments and the ten utterances are all one, how can it be said, in the case of the Commandments, that [Tiferet and Malkhut] were united and that the Shekhinah was driven out? For certainly, once she was united in the coupling she was not diminished, so long as she was in her husband's bosom. And if she was below, why are they ten? For Da'at was by then concealed, and it was not fitting for it to speak a Commandment [dibbur], since it had already been concealed and the matter had not returned to its rectification.

And further: can we say that, had there been no diminishment, the utterances would have been only nine? I wonder at this; for the world would then have lacked, from its perfection, everything that belongs to that one utterance.

And further: since Da'at includes Malkhut and Tiferet, then, as to the utterance that it spoke, by which that creation was created — why did it not create everything that was possible by the power of Malkhut and everything that was possible by the power of Tiferet, seeing that it is the mode of existence of their union, which is their being two great luminaries? And why was there still a creation left over for Malkhut and Tiferet afterward? Was the power of Da'at lacking, when it is more perfect than both of them?

And further: we have several clear proofs that "In the beginning" is the utterance of the supernal Keter. First, in Sefer ha-Bahir, and these are its words: "What are the utterances? The first is the supernal Keter, blessed is it and blessed," etc.; "Chokhmah is the second, as it is written," etc. Thus it counted the supernal Keter among the utterances, and it is the first of them all.

And further: the difficulty is no difficulty to begin with, and proves nothing. For although the word "In the beginning" [bereshit] is in Chokhmah, the utterance is nevertheless in Keter. And because of the fineness of Keter and its nearness to its source — so that, of the four-letter Name, nothing was attributed to it but the thorn of the yod; and it is likewise called alef, from the word pele ['wonder'], and it is called "a wondrous and concealed Amon" [amon: 'nursling' or 'master craftsman'] — although the bet of bereshit is the allusion to Chokhmah, its thorn nevertheless points to Keter. And so Rabbi Akiva explained, and these are his words: "They say to the bet, 'Who created you?' and it points with its thorn to the alef." The meaning is that the bet itself — which is Chokhmah to the existents [havayot], and which is not the start of the Emanation but a second emanation — has a thorn behind it pointing to the alef, as though indicating to those who ask it "Who created you?" (that is, whether it was emanated by something emanated or by a first Emanator); and it shows with its thorn that it is a second emanation, and that the alef, which is Keter, preceded it. And so it can now properly be said that the utterance "In the beginning" is in Keter, although the word bereshit alludes to Chokhmah, since Keter too is somewhat alluded to in it, as we explained. And the point is that the whole Emanation is included in the verse "In the beginning," to indicate of it [Keter] that it is the Emanator — that is, by the power of the Ein Sof — and yet Keter itself is the Emanator and the agent that speaks the utterance. And so we find that most of the utterances are composed of all ten; and that is why an allusion to Chokhmah came in the word bereshit, although the principal part of the utterance is in Keter. Nor is this surprising: for the blessing of the Patriarchs is in Chesed, and yet Chesed is not mentioned in it until "God of Abraham" — and even "God of Abraham" is in Chokhmah — and it is not mentioned in itself except in the words "the great God," apart from the closing formula. So it is with the utterance "In the beginning": granted that the word bereshit is in Chokhmah, the principal part of the utterance is nevertheless in Keter, which is concealed, as is its way; and yet it came by allusion in the thorn of the bet, as we explained — and what is meant is the Chokhmah-within-Keter.

And further, apart from this, it may be said that the bet itself alludes to Keter. The support for this is that the bet of bereshit is the alef of Avgitatz, which is the forty-two-letter Name, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Particulars of the Names, with the help of God; and Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained that the alef of Avgitatz is the allusion to Keter, and these are his words (in Tikkun 70, fol. 116): "The alef of Avgitatz is Keter, wondrous, an Amon, and concealed."

Thus he testified explicitly that the bet of bereshit is in Keter. And close to this is the view of the Ramban, of blessed memory, in Parashat Bereshit, and these are his words: "And the word bereshit alludes to Chokhmah, which is the beginning of beginnings, as I have mentioned; and therefore the Jerusalem Targum rendered it 'with wisdom' [be-chokhmeta]. And the word is crowned with the crown of the bet." Thus far [his] words.

And the meaning of his words is that the bet alludes to Keter, because it is a house [bayit] for all the Sefirot. And this is evident from his wording, for he says "and the word bereshit alludes to Chokhmah": he means the word bereshit — not the bet, but the word itself — as he concludes, "which is the beginning [reshit]," etc.; he did not say that it is called bereshit, but reshit alone. And when he brings proof from the Targum, which rendered "with wisdom" [be-chokhmeta], it is not that [the bet] is actually Chokhmah; rather, the bet of bereshit is a prefix. For the word reshit is Chokhmah and the bet of bereshit is Keter; and that is why he said, "and the word is crowned with the crown of the bet."

From all this it appears that this passage gives no compelling proof for the view of Rabbi Shem Tov, of blessed memory. But it still remains our duty to explain what is found to conflict with this passage in the Zohar, Parashat Vayikra. For in this passage it said that "In the beginning" is the tenth utterance, whereas in Parashat Vayikra (fol. 11b) Rashbi explained that there are ten utterances apart from "In the beginning." And these are his words: "Rabbi Shimon said: It is written, 'Ten, ten the spoon, by the shekel of the sanctuary.' Why 'ten, ten'? Ten for the account of Creation and ten for the giving of the Torah: ten utterances in the account of Creation and ten utterances in the giving of the Torah. What does this tell us? That the world was created only for the sake of the Torah; for as long as Israel occupy themselves with the Torah the world endures, and whenever Israel neglect the Torah, what is written? 'If not for My covenant by day and by night, I would not have set the laws of heaven and earth.' Come and see: ten utterances for the account of Creation, as we have learned, 'By ten utterances the world was created'; ten utterances for the giving of the Torah, these being the Ten Commandments. It is written, 'I am YHVH your God,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let there be light, and there was light.' This (is) the faith of the Holy One, blessed be He, [who] is called 'light,' as it is written, 'YHVH is my light and my salvation,' etc. It is written, 'You shall have no other gods before Me,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters,' etc. 'Let there be a firmament': this is Israel, who are the portion of the Holy One, blessed be He, and who hold fast to that place called 'heaven.' And this is the secret: once Rabbi Yeisa the Elder asked Rabbi Ila'i, saying: All the other nations the Holy One, blessed be He, gave over to great appointed rulers; where are Israel? He sent back to him: 'And God set them in the firmament of heaven.' And he sent him a good answer. 'In the midst of the waters': amid the words of the Torah. 'And let it divide between waters and waters': between the Holy One, blessed be He, who is called 'a well of living waters,' and idolatry, which is called 'broken cisterns that can hold no water,' which are the bitter waters, etc., foul and stagnant. Therefore holy Israel divide between waters and waters. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not take the name of YHVH your God in vain,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let the waters under the heaven be gathered to one place.' Come and see: whoever swears falsely by the holy Name, it is as though he separated the Mother [Imma] from her place above, and the holy crowns are not settled in their places, as it is said, 'and a whisperer separates the Chief [aluf],' and the 'Chief' is none other than the Holy One, blessed be He. And it is written, 'Let the waters under the heaven be gathered to one place': do not make a separation through a false oath. 'To one place': as is fitting, in the place of truth, and not in another place, for falsehood. And what is falsehood? When the waters go to another place that is not theirs. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let the earth sprout grass, herb.' When did the holy earth grow great and become crowned with her crowns? You must say, on the Sabbath day; for then the bride is joined to the King, to bring forth grasses and blessings for the world. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven.' What does this tell us? That these luminaries are 'your father and your mother': 'your father' is the sun, 'your mother' is the moon. And the sun is none other than the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written, 'For YHVH Elohim is a sun and a shield'; and the moon is none other than the Assembly of Israel, as it is written, 'and your moon shall not withdraw.' Therefore all is one. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not murder,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let the waters swarm with living souls.' And you: do not kill a human being, who is called by that name, as it is written, 'and the man became a living soul.' Do not be like those fish, of whom the great swallow the small. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not commit adultery,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let the earth bring forth living souls after their kind.' From here we learn that a man must not be false with another woman who is not his mate; and therefore it is written, 'Let the earth bring forth living souls after their kind': that a woman should bear only from her own kind. And who is her kind? Her mate. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not steal,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'And God said: Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed.' What I have given you and entrusted to you shall be yours; and you shall not steal what belongs to another. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'And God said: Let us make man in our image.' Against one who is in the image of the King, do not bear false witness; and whoever bears false witness against his fellow, it is as though he bore [false] witness above. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not covet your neighbor's wife,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'It is not good that the man should be alone.' See, your mate is there before you; therefore 'you shall not covet your neighbor's wife.' And these are the ten utterances for the account of Creation and the ten utterances for the giving of the Torah; and this is what is written, 'Ten, ten the spoon, by the shekel of the sanctuary': they were weighed as one, in a single balance. And for this reason the world stands and peace is found in it." Thus far [his] words.

And from it, it appears explicitly that among the ten utterances of the account of Creation, "In the beginning" is not an utterance at all; and this is certainly a difficulty. And in order to understand this matter we shall first set down another passage, from the Tikkunim, and through it this perplexity will be cleared up, with the help of God.

In the Tikkunim it is implied that the work of the utterances was not done by any of the first three; for the first utterance, which is Keter, is "Let there be light"; the second utterance, Chokhmah, is "Let there be a firmament"; and the third utterance, Binah, is "Let the waters be gathered." And these are its words (in Tikkun 42, fol. 79): "Bereshit: there [in that word] is ish ['man'], of whom it is said, 'and Jacob was a whole man [ish tam]'; and this is the third day, for there were three craftsmen up to this point: the first day, the second day and the third day, each of which brought forth its craft. To the first day spoke that wondrous and concealed Amon, that grade which is called Ayin ['Nothing'] and comprises three Sefirot — alef, Keter; yod, Chokhmah; nun, Binah — etc. It told each of the three days to bring forth its craft. It said to the first day, 'Let there be light'; at once it brought forth its craft and made it, as it is written, 'and there was light.' And they have established that there is no 'being' [havayah] except through making [asiyah]. The alef of Ayin, which was flying in the air [avir], brought forth light [or]; the yod brought forth the firmament; the nun of Ayin brought forth the dry land, as it is written, 'And God said: Let the waters be gathered,' etc." Thus far [its] words.

From it, it appears explicitly that those who acted were the craftsmen, which are the six days, and that they acted at the utterance of the first three, which are Ayin. And among the things that should also be understood about these utterances is that they are ten; and although they are ten, we know that there is no creation and no action except through the six days alone, which are: Gedulah, the first day; Gevurah, the second day; Tiferet, the third day; Netzach, the fourth day; Hod, the fifth day; Yesod, the sixth day. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained: that the whole work of Creation was included in and done through these days, in Malkhut, and Malkhut brings the things out into the light in completeness. And these are his words in Parashat Terumah (fol. 127): "'Of the trees of Lebanon': these are the planted trees that the Holy One, blessed be He, uprooted and transplanted in another place; and these are called 'cedars of Lebanon,' as it is said, 'the cedars of Lebanon that He planted.' And this palanquin was built and completed only through them. Again, 'of the trees of Lebanon': these are the six days of Creation. Each and every day arranges in this palanquin the arrangement that is proper to it. The first arrangement: there flowed from the right side the primordial light that was hidden away, and it was taken from the right side; and there entered into this palanquin a certain image, in the likeness of this light, by means of a certain Foundation [Yesod], and it performed its service in it. Afterward this palanquin brought forth a certain image in the likeness of this light. And this is the secret of what is written, 'Let there be light, and there was light.' Since it said 'Let there be light,' why is it written 'and there was light'? Scripture needed only to write 'and it was so.' What is 'and there was light'? It is that this light brought forth another light that was proper to it. And this is the first day of those trees of Lebanon. The second arrangement: there flowed from the left side the separation of the waters, in a flow of mighty fire; it was taken from the left side and entered into that palanquin and performed its service in it, and it separated the waters on the right side from the waters on the left side. Afterward that palanquin brought forth a certain image in its likeness. And this is the secret of what is written, 'between the waters that are under the firmament and the waters that are above the firmament; and it was so.' And this is the second day of those trees of Lebanon. The third arrangement: there flowed from the left side and from the right side a certain third day, which makes peace in the world; and from there fruits were drawn. And this one performed its service in this palanquin and brought forth kind after its kind: a kind for many works, the kind that was proper to it, and all the grasses and herbs and trees, in their many powers. And its image remained there, and that palanquin brought forth a kind in that very likeness. And this is the third day, which is composed of two sides, of those trees of Lebanon. The fourth arrangement: the light of the sun flowed and shone, to give light to this palanquin within its darkness; and it entered into it to give light, but performed no service in it until the fifth day, when this palanquin brought forth that service of the light that had entered it on the fourth day; and that palanquin brought forth in the very likeness of that light. And this is the fourth day, one of those trees of Lebanon. The fifth arrangement: there flowed a certain current of the swarming of the waters, and it performed its service, to bring forth the light of the arrangement of the fourth day; it performed its service in this palanquin and brought forth kinds after their kind, those that appear in that very likeness. And this day performed that service more than all the other days. And all remained in suspense until the sixth day, when this palanquin brought forth all that was stored up in it, as it is written, 'Let the earth bring forth living souls after their kind.' And this is the fifth day, one of those trees of Lebanon. The sixth arrangement: this is the day on which this whole palanquin was arrayed; it has no arraying and no strength except from this day. When this [day] came, it arrayed this palanquin with many spirits, with many souls, with many maidens fair to behold, such as are fit to dwell in the palace of the King. It too was arrayed in the beauty [of] all the other days that had gone before, and it arrayed them in one desire, in delight, in joy: an arraying of above and below. Then this palanquin was sanctified with supernal sanctities and crowned with its crowns, until it rose in the ascent of the crown of rest and was called by a supernal name, a holy name, which is Sabbath: the rest of all, the desire of all, the cleaving of all, above and below as one. And then it is written, 'King Solomon made himself a palanquin of the trees of Lebanon.'" Thus far [his] words.

And although the passage needs a long explanation, as will be given in Sefer Or Yakar, with God's help, it is nevertheless explicitly implied in it that all the utterances and the creations were through the six days: "Let there be light, and there was light" is in Chesed, etc. It turns out that, even if we say that "In the beginning" is an utterance, nothing at all is left for the first three. Therefore we must clear the stumbling-stones of the difficulties from these passages and set this discussion on its proper footing.
