"And a river issues from Eden to water," etc.—"that river that flows and issues," etc. He said "flows" because Eden is Binah, and the river is Tiferet, and the garden is Malkhut; and because it does not water the garden as [soon as] it issues from its mother's womb—for it must be drawn a journey of five hundred years, that is, the five Sefirot, until it arrives to water the garden—therefore he was compelled to use the language "flows," that is, meaning: it is drawn through all those grades until it arrives at the garden. And he reversed the order in saying "flows" and afterward "issues," because it was difficult for him that it would have been fitting for the verse to be silent about the word "issues" and say "a river from Eden waters the garden," since the word "issues" is not precise—for it issues and is drawn [onward]; or let it say "and a river issues from Eden and comes to water the garden," for now the language of each one would be precise, that is, [that it is] drawn. And at the resolution of this he aimed in saying "flows and issues"; namely, that the verse comes to inform us of a novel matter: that we should not err and say that when Tiferet waters Malkhut it does not actually water [her] from the effluence of Binah, but changes it from its nature and waters Malkhut according to her measure below. For this he said that it is not so; rather, Tiferet pours into Malkhut that effluence according to its nature in Binah, as though Malkhut herself were receiving from Binah itself, with no intermediary at all. And this is what it says: "issues from Eden to water the garden." And therefore it did not say "and comes," because the matter of the drawing-forth does not intrinsically pertain here, since it is not changed from its character on account of the drawing-forth—as though the garden, which is Malkhut, actually receives it from the source, which is Binah, and Tiferet and Yesod serve for this matter of watering only the service of a passage. And this he taught us by his language "flows and issues"—the intent [being]: as is the mode of its issuing from Binah, so is the mode of its being drawn forth. And the measure of the language is thus: it flows in the mode in which it issues, and in the mode in which it issues it enters the garden—as though she herself were receiving from Binah with no intermediary. And this is what he says: "and waters it with the watering from above." The intent is that the effluence that comes to her by means of the river is as though she were drawing sustenance and receiving from Binah itself with no intermediary—"the watering from above," actually; and the intermediaries serve for this matter only the service of a mere channel, although it is not so with regard to other matters and to another effluence. "And gives it rest"—the intent is that Yesod makes rest for Malkhut by this effluence, and no benefit is drawn from it to Yesod; because this effluence is to rectify Malkhut and to adorn her, alone. For this effluence is like the first rainfall [revi'ah] upon the earth, which is for the preparing of the ground, to plough and to sow, and not to make what is sown grow. And therefore he said "and gives it rest"—meaning that this benefit is for Malkhut alone. But after this rectification he pours into her the effluence that is fit to beget, which is the coupling after the rectification and the adornment of the bride. And then the effluence is to make fruit, which are the souls that are poured forth from above in the secret of the union of the groom and his bride. And this is "and it yields fruit"—for the souls are the fruit of the Tree; and this is the matter of the second rainfall, which is to make the existence of the seeds sprout. "And makes seeds grow"—this is the matter of the third rainfall, which is the effluence poured forth to make grow and to make splendid the plantings and the seeds, which are the souls; and this is "and makes seeds grow." And they are a parable for marital relations in the last three months, of which it is explained in the Gemara (Niddah, fol. 31a) that they are good for the child and for the mother—namely, that the child comes forth vigorous. And from our flesh we behold God: for so it is above—when the effluence increases upon the plantings, the plantings multiply and grow. And the witness to this is the matter of the soul that comes in the waning of the moon or in its fullness, expounded in the words of Rashbi in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 69, fol. 98). "And it is then rest for all"—meaning: when the effluence is in these two times, which are the second and the third rainfall, then by this benefit and rest are drawn to all: to Tiferet and Yesod, which are the secret of the river and the secret of the male, and to Malkhut, which is the secret of the female, as is known. For in the coupling there is rest for the male and rest for the female, in the secret of "the Shekhinah among the lower beings is a supernal need." "And this is rest for the garden, and this one makes rest in it." He aimed to explain that, although we say "and this is rest for all," the intent is not that it is rest for them equally. Rather, the rest of the Shekhinah is drawn from the river itself; and this is what he says, "and this is rest for the garden"—by means of the said river there is benefit and repose for the Shekhinah. But it is not the rest of the river, [in the sense] that the Shekhinah makes repose for him; rather, it is drawn to him from above on her account. And this is what he says, "and this one makes rest in it"—meaning, the river makes repose, respite and ease in her; and not that she makes the repose for him. Rather, he makes his rest there, and the rest is drawn to him from above on her account, through the river's coupling, until abundant effluence is drawn to him from above. And it is a parable of a weary man who stops to rest in some place: it is not the place that makes rest for him, but he makes his rest there. "As it is said, 'for in it He rested,'" etc. Neither of the verses is specific to his proof, for each of them admits of being explained in two ways. Either we say [that] "for in it He rested" means: [she] rested in Yesod, and not [in] Malkhut; or we say [that] "in it" means: in the garden, which is Malkhut, Yesod rested and reposed. And so the verse "and He rested on the seventh day"—we can explain it in these two ways: the one, meaning that Yesod rested in Malkhut, which is the Sabbath day; or it means that Malkhut rested on the seventh day, which is Yesod—for of both of them the name "seventh day" is correctly predicated, as we shall explain in the Values of the Allusions, under the heading "Sabbath" and under the heading "days." And he aimed to explain from these two verses the two aspects—the rest of Malkhut and the rest of Yesod—for from the superfluity of the verses we expound one thus and one thus; for if you do not say so, why are [both] needed? Rather, [it is] as we have explained. And because on the face of it one [sense] is implied—namely, that Malkhut rested and reposed in Yesod, which on the face of it is the more accepted—therefore he took up first the second verse and said "for in it He rested," that is, the additional verse, which comes to teach us the resting of Yesod in Malkhut; for the resting of Malkhut in Yesod is the first verse, which is "and He rested on the seventh day." And this is what he aimed at in reversing the order of the verses—as if he said: Know that Yesod rested and reposed in Malkhut, for it is written "for in it He rested." What will you say—that this is the resting of Malkhut in Yesod? For this he said, "and He rested on the seventh day," meaning the resting of Malkhut in Yesod—behold, it is [already] written; for they are two verses: the first for the resting of Malkhut in Yesod, and the second for the resting of Yesod in Malkhut. This is the way according to this reading, and it is the more correct reading. And there are books that read, above: "and makes seeds grow, and it is then rest for the garden, and the garden is rest in it, as it is written, 'for in it He rested,'" etc. And it is possible to settle it [thus]: that the intent, with regard to the union, is the two aspects in Malkhut—her mode of existence that is united with her husband, which ascends to be united, and her mode of existence that remains in its place, in the secret of the modes of existence.

And behold, the mode of existence that ascends—its rest is in her husband himself, who is united with it. And her lower mode of existence has rest, but not in her husband himself, for he is not united with it but with the upper mode of existence alone. And of these two aspects he spoke. Of the aspect that remains, which is the lower aspect, he said "and it is then rest for the garden"—meaning: repose and contentment are drawn to the garden, but not that her rest is with him himself. And of the second aspect he said "and the garden is rest in it," that is, in him himself—which is the mode of existence that ascends to be united. And he brought proof for this matter from the two verses. First, "for in it He rested," that is, in him himself, in the secret of the aspect that is united with her husband above. And the second, "and He rested on the seventh day," which means that He poured forth rest upon the seventh day; but it is not evident from it that [it is] in him himself, as [in] the first verse, which said "for in it He rested," that is, in him himself. And therefore he put first the verse "for in it He rested," because from it it is compelled that "and He rested on the seventh day" is not in him himself—since it did not say "in it" in that verse. "The secret of the matter," etc.—meaning, the sum of the secret of the whole matter is that there is none who gives contentment to Malkhut but Yesod, in the secret of the river from its beginning to its end, that is, the vav, which is the river, as is well known. And by this the word "These" will be understood: for the intent is not "these are generations, and not others"—for there are no others besides them—but this is its explanation: "These are the generations of Noah"—Noah is the master of generations, and none other. And the word "These," which invalidates, does not invalidate generations; rather, it invalidates [another] master of generations—for there is no master of generations but Yesod. And this is what is meant by "the secret of the matter," etc. "Come and see: in like manner, Noah below was the holy covenant." Now he comes to explain "Noah, Noah," which means two rests, as explained above. And to indicate that the intent is Yesod, which is what is alluded to in Noah, he said "Noah was the holy covenant"—meaning: Noah was the chariot for Yesod, which is kayyama kaddisha, whose meaning is "holy covenant." "And therefore he is called 'a man of the ground'"—meaning, husband [ba'al] of the ground; the intent is: husband of Malkhut, who is called "ground." "And we have learned a secret: for Noah," etc. He wished to prove that Yesod has no place into which to pour except Malkhut—lest we say that it is true that Malkhut does not receive from any but Yesod, yet it is still possible that Yesod pours into something other than Malkhut. For this he said, "we have learned a secret," etc., "Noah needed the ark," etc.—the intent being that just as Malkhut needs Yesod, so Yesod needs Malkhut; as he goes on to explain, that there is no subsistence for the generations of Yesod except by means of Malkhut, as he concludes. "Who is the ark? This is the Ark of the Covenant," etc. It was difficult for him, for the correlation of the ark, which is Malkhut, is correlated only with the aspect of Yesod, which is Noah. For [it is] like the head-tefillin, which is the male, and the female correlated with it is the hand-tefillin; and so day in relation to night, and so the sun in relation to the moon, and so the etrog with the species that are in the lulav. And therefore it would be fitting, since Noah is Yesod, that his wife be Malkhut, and she is a correlative aspect. But that Noah, who is a human being, should be correlated with an ark of gopher wood—this is certainly not correlative. For this he said that, on the contrary, the aspect of Malkhut in respect of Yesod is found only in the ark. And the proof is from the Ark where the Torah is: Scripture called it "the Ark of the Covenant"—meaning that Malkhut is called "ark" [aron] and "ark" [tevah] in respect of her joining to Yesod, and this is "the Ark of the Covenant." And now, since Noah is Yesod, that which is correlated with Yesod, which is Noah, is none but the ark. And this is what he says: "And Noah and the ark below were thus, after the pattern of above"—meaning, they are correlated, even though Noah is a human being and this is an ark of wood. And he proved the matter from Scripture, in his saying "Of Noah, 'covenant' is written"—meaning, Scripture testified to his being a chariot for Yesod, as [in] "and I will establish My covenant with you," etc. "And until the covenant was established in him," etc.—meaning: after he proved that Noah is Yesod, he wished to prove also that the ark is Malkhut; and this is what he says, "and until the covenant was established in him"—meaning: since we see that he did not merit to enter the ark until he was at the grade of covenant, it appears that the ark is Malkhut, and he did not merit to enter within Malkhut until he was "covenant," which is Yesod. And this is what Scripture says: "and I will establish My covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark"—meaning: when I establish My covenant with you, that is, that he be a chariot for Yesod, then he will merit to enter within the ark, which is Malkhut. "And then the ark was the Ark of the Covenant"—meaning: when Noah, who is called "covenant," is within the ark, then the ark is called the Ark of the Covenant. And [so] the matter of the ark and Noah is settled—their being correlated with one another in a complete relation. And this is what he says: "Ark and Noah—all after the manner of above," etc.—meaning: just as Noah did not enter the ark until he was "covenant," it appears that Malkhut has no effluence or receiving except from Yesod. And since, in order to keep seed alive, he needed to enter the ark, it appears that Yesod has no place apart from Malkhut. And the intent in this is to explain to us what Scripture said, "These," which invalidated the former ones: that there is none who pours into Malkhut but Yesod, and Yesod has no recipient but Malkhut. And this is "Ark and Noah—all after the manner of above," as explained: that there is no livelihood or subsistence or generations for Noah except by means of the ark, and there is no existence for the ark except through Noah. "Noah was a righteous man—so it is, certainly, after the manner," etc. It was difficult for him: according to what he has now explained—that the intent of Scripture in the matter of "These are the generations of Noah: Noah" is Yesod, which makes generations, and it invalidated [any other], for no other makes generations; and it said twice "Noah, Noah," which are two rests, rest for Malkhut and rest for Yesod—if so, it is difficult, for the verse is superfluous in saying "a righteous man." And he explained that the aspect of his being called "righteous" is not the same as the aspect of his being called "Noah." For he is called "Noah" on account of the generations and the souls, as explained at the beginning of our discussion; but he is called "righteous" from his aspect of being the subsistence of Malkhut—that is to say, from the aspect of Yesod's pouring into Malkhut the effluence without which she has no subsistence. And this is what he says: "So it is, certainly, after the manner of above"—the intent being that just as Yesod has yet another aspect besides the generations, so [too] Noah, who was a chariot for him, [was so] in this aspect as well. And this is what he said, "after the manner of above"—meaning, in all the supernal aspects. "And therefore it is written, 'and the righteous one is the foundation of the world.'" Meaning: he comes to explain that the aspect of Yesod in which it is called "righteous" is on account of Malkhut's having no existence without him—not in the aspect of the souls, but in the aspect of the sustenance and the effluence and the subsistence of Malkhut. And he proved the matter from the verse "and the righteous one is the foundation of the world"; and the intent is that he is the foundation [yesod] of Malkhut, which is the lower world, and she has no existence without him—like a foundation, which is the place of the building and makes it stand, and without which it has no standing or footing. And this is what he says: "and the earth is sustained upon this; for he," etc.—meaning: the existence of the intrinsic subsistence is only by means of Yesod. "And who is he? This is the Righteous One"—meaning: and what is the name and the allusion that delimits and defines this aspect? You must say: "This is the Righteous One"—[the name] alludes to this aspect, as it is written, "and the righteous one is the foundation of the world." If so, it appears of necessity that the word "righteous" alludes to the aspect of the subsistence of Malkhut; and this is what Scripture aimed at in saying "a righteous man"—the intent being that he had the aspect of subsistence as well; that in respect of this aspect too he was a chariot for Yesod. And this is what he says: "And Noah is called 'righteous' below"—meaning that he was a chariot for him in this aspect as well. "And the secret of all," etc.—meaning: he proved the matter from Scripture, which said "Noah walked." And if it should arise in the mind that Noah was a chariot for Yesod only in respect of the generations alone, why did Scripture say "with God," etc.—whose intent is that his walking was always with the Shekhinah, who is called "God" [Elohim]? For the aspect of the generations is only from time to time. Rather, certainly [it is] as we have said. "'With God,' etc.—that he never separated from Him"—meaning that the Shekhinah is always with Yesod in union. It appears that he was a chariot also in respect of the perpetual effluence that is poured forth for sustenance. And therefore it is fitting that she not be separated from him, for she has no existence without him. "And [so as] to be on earth after the manner of above"—meaning, in all the aspects that are in Yesod, as explained. "'A righteous man'—the foundation of the world; 'covenant of peace,'" etc. It was difficult for him: granted that it should say "righteous," as we have said—what does "man" come for? For "man" is the very same as "righteous," that is, "husband," as in the saying "the man of God," which means husband of the Shekhinah. For this he resolved that "man" is another aspect besides these two; namely, that Yesod is called "man" when the Shekhinah is clothed in the force of judgment, when she is a sword of war; and Yesod pours into her and sets the blood of war in peace—then he is called "man." And this is what he says, "covenant of peace"—meaning, Yesod is called "covenant of peace"; and his being called "covenant of peace" is in this aspect: that he brings peace to the world, which exists in the force of the judgment that is poured forth from Malkhut reddened with judgment. And this is what he says, "the peace of the world"—in this aspect Noah is called "man." And this is what he says of Noah himself: "'a man of the ground'—certainly"; the intent being that he is "man" and pours forth peace and mercy when Malkhut is called "ground" [adamah]—the intent being: when she is red [adumah], from the side of the force of the redness of judgment. And it is an aspect new beyond the two preceding ones. "And therefore, 'and Noah found favor,'" etc.—meaning: because Noah was a chariot for Yesod from the side of all these aspects, it was said, of the rank of his chariot-hood, "and Noah found favor"—which was not said of any other. For how many others there were who were a chariot for Yesod, and "found favor" was not said of them! Rather, certainly the reason is that he included all the aspects that Yesod has with Malkhut, which is not so with the others. Thus far the explanation of the passage. And the general rule that emerges from the passage is that Yesod pours into Malkhut, and Malkhut does not receive from any other. And by this the view of those who say that there are two channels from Netzach and Hod to Malkhut is annulled; rather, it is impossible for any Sefirah among the Sefirot to pour into Malkhut except by means of Yesod. Further, Scripture said (Isaiah 57), "and none understands that because of the evil the righteous one is gathered in"—meaning, gathered in from pouring forth. It appears that all the effluence depends on Yesod, which is the Righteous One; for if not so, how did it say that the righteous one alone "is gathered in"? And so they expounded of the Assembly of Israel, which is Malkhut, that she is likened to a dove, etc. And so it is said (Isaiah 57:1), "The righteous one has lost," etc.—he has lost the Lady [Matronita]. And the like. All this indicates that there is none who pours into Malkhut but Yesod. And it is indeed true that we find that Netzach pours into Malkhut, and likewise Hod; and likewise, above, in the matter of the thread of lovingkindness from the side of Chesed, and the scarlet thread from the side of Gevurah. The intent is not that they have other channels; rather, the intent is that all is by means of Yesod, which is the passage for all sustenance and effluence that is poured into Malkhut. And just as we insist upon this of her, so we insist in the matter of Yesod, that he has no place into which to pour but her, as is proved from the passage mentioned above.

A further channel is drawn from Yesod to Malkhut; for it is the course of the great river that issues from the Edens [delights] of Binah to water the garden. And by means of this channel he takes hold of Malkhut, to couple her with her husband above; and by way of this channel she was driven out, through iniquities. And concerning this channel we have seen in the Ta'amei ha-Mitzvot of Ibn Farchi, in the negative commandment not to drink libation-wine [yein nesekh], and these are his words there: "There are two orifices in the supernal Covenant. From the one he pours to the Shekhinah, and that effluence which goes out is called 'sweet waters'; and from there go out many reasons [te'amim, 'flavors'] of Torah, which are called 'water,' as it is said (Isaiah 55:1), 'Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the water'—and 'water' is nothing but Torah. And the second orifice pours to the powers of impurity, and it is called 'libation-wine,'" etc. Thus far his words, in brief.
Behold, from his language it is implied that these words of his are words of received tradition [kabbalah]. And the matters prove themselves of their own accord, for "from my flesh I behold God."

And behold, in a human being there are two orifices: the one to pour into his female, to beget in his likeness, and the second to expel the foul matter and the residue. Further, we have found a companion for him in a book whose author's name is not known to us—it is a commentary on the Song of Songs and a commentary on Parashat Terumah, and its language in some places is Aramaic—and these are its words, in the explanation of the letters, on the letter ayin: "And now we have to show, in the secret of ayin—their source—what the image is; thus it hints: secrets hinted and hidden were engraved. Beneath the chariot of the Holy King is the secret of the holy covenant of the Holy One, blessed be He, which is called 'the righteous one, the foundation of the world'; and it is the wellspring that pours into the holy well, which is the Lady.

"And those two heads of the ayin are the secret of these two orifices that are in the mouth of the member. And they are two wellsprings: the holy wellspring of the right is the nourishment of the Lady, and from there draw nourishment the prophets and the pious and the blameless and the righteous, who delight in the Garden of Eden. And the second wellspring is the nourishment of the bands of impurity and of the angels that accuse in the world; and from there is the nourishment of Balaam the wicked; and from there comes the good [fortune] of the wicked, who prosper in their ways in this world. And concerning this it is written (Job 38:13), 'and the wicked are shaken out of it'—with a large ayin—for their nourishment is from the second head of the ayin." Thus far [its] words.

And his words are clear, being a support for the tradition of Ibn Farchi that I wrote above, who said that in Yesod there are two channels, one holy and one for the dross, the smeltings of gold. He further wrote these very things in the explanation of the letter tzadi: "The tzadi has two heads, which hints at the attribute of the Righteous One [tzaddik]; and those are two holy wellsprings. One pours and draws from there to the Lady, and from there the upper and the lower ones are blessed—'for there YHVH commanded the blessing,' etc. And this is the wellspring from which the holy angels were created, and many holy souls were created. And the second wellspring pours to His left side (of the Holy One, blessed be He), and from there is the nourishment of the strange woman and the adulterous woman. And if Israel are worthy, that wellspring is stopped up and the holy wellspring of the right is opened; and if not, that wellspring is opened which pours [to] the strange woman—the powers of impurity that sit outside the supernal academy, which are called 'others' [acherim]," etc. "And from the second wellspring—from there go out [draw nourishment] demons and spirits and night-spirits [lilin] and harmful beings and the wicked, from the left side," etc. Thus far [its] words.

And his words are clear and agree with our matter. And there is some proof for this in the Zohar, Parashat Acharei (fol. 74a), and these are its words: "Rabbi Yehudah said: At the time when the righteous multiply in the world, the Assembly of Israel sends up good fragrances and is blessed by the Holy King, and her face shines. And at the time when the wicked multiply in the world, as it were, the Assembly of Israel does not send up fragrance, and she tastes of the bitter Other Side [Sitra Achra]. Then it is written, 'He cast down from heaven to earth the beauty [tiferet] of Israel,' and her face is darkened." Thus far [its] words.

And the intent is that when there are in this world righteous and pious ones, then by means of their good deeds the Shekhinah draws effluence from above through their merit; and they are the female waters [mayin nukvin] that she pours forth in order to receive the male waters [mayin dekhurin], as we shall explain in the Gate of Essence and Governance, with God's help. And so is the matter with regard to the effluence and the blessing. And this is what it says, "sends up fragrances"—meaning, she sends up the fragrance of the deeds of the righteous, as in the matter of (Genesis 27:27) "See, the fragrance of my son is as the fragrance of a field"—for he smelled in him that it was from the supernal field. And when there are no righteous in this world, the effluence does not descend, and Malkhut seeks the waters of lovingkindness [chesed] and there are none. And then the power of judgment is aroused through the claims of the husks, and they are poured upon by way of that evil channel; and then she tastes [what is] more bitter than death. And this is "and she tastes of the Other Side," etc.—meaning, she tastes bitterness from the place of gall, from impurity. And accordingly it is compelled that there be in Yesod two channels: one for blessing, from the side of the right, and one for bitterness, from the side of the left, by which dross is poured to her, from the side of the smeltings of gold, and she receives bitter dross. And one who has eyes of intellect and is of the reapers of the field will understand, by this premise, the matter of the sin of the son of the Israelite woman (Leviticus 24), which is sealed in the Zohar, and they revealed it to those who know; and we shall not explain, because "it is the glory of God to conceal a matter." And the matter will be understood when you are precise about the language of the Zohar in Parashat Emor (fol. 106a), which said there, "the last heh was the female," etc. And with this he was covering over his mother, and he cursed himself, God forbid. "But we will bless Yah." And the reason for there being in the Righteous One these two orifices is that the Righteous One was the governor who poured forth to the upper and the lower, to the inner and to the outer ones, and on him hung the sustenance of all creatures, those of the right and those of the left, before the diminishment; and also whenever Malkhut ascends to her place, to the height [ha-Ramatah], to her husband, for there is her house—sitting at the head of the corner, as will be explained in the Gate of the Diminishment [of the Moon]—then it is compelled that the Righteous One be the one who feeds the world; and then the creatures are poured upon by means of these two orifices: the one for the sustenance, to the sons of the palace, and the second, the residue, to the dogs. And if the questioner should ask, "Who has put residue among the holy things?"—this will be explained in the Gate of the Substitutions. And in these matters brevity is fitting, out of regard for the honor of the Omnipresent.

After we have, in the preceding chapters, summed up the tradition of the channels as it is found in the mouth of all the Kabbalists, early and late, we shall now broaden the explanation and explain the matter of these channels according to their aspect, and according to what is understood by us from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, after the whole of the Values of the Allusions, with their explanation, has passed through our mind—as their aspect and their division and their matter will be explained. And after looking into the matter of the bond of the Sefirot according to Rashbi, as will be explained in the Gate of Essence and Governance—and there it is explained that they are bound by means of their equivalents; that is to say, that Keter is united with the nine Sefirot by means of the portion of Keter that is in all the Sefirot, and Chokhmah by means of the portion of Chokhmah that is in all the Sefirot, and Binah by means of the portion of Binah that is in all the Sefirot. And after the intellect has been well strengthened in this premise, by the power of inquiry and correct discernment, as will be explained in the Gate of Essence and Governance, the inquirer will discern with his intellect that the channels vary according to the aspects, by the thousands and the myriads, just as the inclusions of the Sefirot have no number. And the example of this: when the faces turn, and the face of Keter shines upon Chokhmah with the shining face that is in it from the side of its own self, Keter, then it is compelled that Chokhmah show opposite it a face correlative to the face of Keter [which is the Keter-within-Chokhmah]; and then they are united and bound in a mighty union and bond, by means of the shining of the faces and the drawing-forth of the light, in the likeness of the light that goes out from the eye, as explained above at the beginning of chapter one. And this is a superior union, by means of which Chokhmah receives the names [effluence] of Keter and its very aspect, because their union and their channel are by means of Keter itself, pouring and receiving; and this is the most superior union among all the unions. And then three aspects are distinguished between them, besides the three aspects mentioned above, as explained. And these aspects are: the aspect of the Keter that pours, and the aspect of the Keter that receives, and the aspect of the middle channel between them, which raises the light and pours it—behold, their union is complete. And at times they are united by means of the aspects of Chokhmah. The example of this: that Keter reveals the face of Chokhmah that it has, in order to pour into Chokhmah; and then Chokhmah reveals its face, the face of Chokhmah that it has; and then they are united in a mighty union by means of the faces that are equal, for good; and there comes to be between them the channel that befits them, according to the aspect of their union.

And behold, this union is superior, but not as the first. For in the first, of which we said that the union is by means of Keter, Chokhmah receives from Keter effluence as befits Keter—for from Keter to Keter all is poured—and it receives a hidden effluence according to the measure of the one that pours and the one that receives. But with Chokhmah, even though it receives a superior effluence, nonetheless it is not as the first, for this is the effluence of Chokhmah, since from Chokhmah to Chokhmah it went forth. And in this way the inquirer shall judge for all the unions that this Sefirah has with the one above it. And from the union of this Sefirah will be understood their union one with another, one with them all and them all with one; and so for all the Sefirot. And now, according to this way, when we wish to pour forth mercy in the secret of the mercies of Keter, we unite Chokhmah with Keter in the aspect of Keter, and Binah with Keter in the aspect of Keter, and Chesed with Chokhmah in the aspect of Keter, and Gevurah with Binah in the aspect of Keter. And let no man's heart fail him at our saying that Binah receives from Keter in the aspect of the Keter that is in it and pours into Gevurah in the aspect of the Keter that is in it; for it is known that their being composed of ten ascends without limit and without end. And it turns out, accordingly, [that there are] how many faces to the awesome faces, and how many backs to the backs that are seen. And when it receives, it receives in the aspect of the Keter-within-Keter-within-Binah; and when it pours, it pours in the aspect of the Keter-within-Malkhut-within-Binah. And so for all the Sefirot. For in this way the aspects will be; and accordingly the pouring-forth is found [to be] the pouring-forth of Keter, from Keter to Keter, down to the last grade among the grades, and the mercy [is] simple mercy, in the manner that befits Keter.

And further, it is fitting that Keter be united in all the Sefirot through the Keter that is in them, at that same moment; and so Chokhmah, and so for all the Sefirot. And then the effluence is an effluence bright and radiant, as the radiance of those that shine. And when, God forbid, judgment is poured forth, then the Sefirot receive from one another by means of the aspect of Gevurah that is in each one of them; and then the judgment is poured forth with force, "and God hastens to do it," and does not delay the day of its coming. And according to this way we may infer to the other actions. And with this premise it will be understood, manifestly, [that there is] a compelling necessity for the governance—as for the actions—of union, in the agreement of all the Sefirot, in the binding of limb to limb and aspect to aspect, until their agreeing together upon that action; and they are all clothed in the likeness of that action and are transformed according to the aspect of their action. And by this the channels vary in their aspect by the thousands and the myriads; for they are always united according to their bond and their union, which is the union of all the aspects and all the divisions in complete equality—and so the channels, for the aspects and the channels are all one thing. And it has been reported to us that there exists a book whose name is Sefer ha-Tzinorot (the Book of the Channels), which speaks of the matter of the channels specifically and counts six hundred thousand channels. And for our iniquities we have not merited it; and they say that it is found among our brethren in the city of Fez, may their Rock and Redeemer preserve them. And it is our wish now to divide the matter of the divisions by which it is possible for the Sefirot to receive one from another: whether from Keter to Keter down to Malkhut, or from Chokhmah to Chokhmah down to Malkhut, or from Binah to Binah down to Malkhut; and so for all the Sefirot—from Chesed to Chesed, and from Gevurah to Gevurah, and from Tiferet to Tiferet, and from Netzach to Netzach, and from Hod to Hod, and from Yesod to Yesod, and from Malkhut to Malkhut. And by this all the Sefirot are found to be in agreement upon one action, in the secret of the channels, all included and in agreement upon that action. And not only this, from Sefirah to Sefirah, but even within a Sefirah itself, in the secret of its pouring into its parts, it will be likewise in this way—for example, from Keter to Keter, and all within Keter. And the inclusions of the ten Sefirot that are in Keter are found all opened and shining with the light of Keter, or with the light of Chokhmah, or with the light of Binah, and so with the other lights that are in the Sefirot; and so for the parts of the other Sefirot—that the Sefirah of Chokhmah be opened entirely in [the light of] Keter, or entirely in the light of Chokhmah, or entirely in the light of Binah, and so with the other lights of the Sefirot.

And behold, there are yet [further] aspects. The example of this: if Keter pours, through the Keter that is in it, into the Chokhmah-within-Chokhmah, and from the Chokhmah-within-Chokhmah into the Binah-within-Binah, and from the Binah-within-Binah into the Chesed-within-Chesed, and so for all the Sefirot in this way—there are many kinds of divisions, which it is impossible to grasp except by a corporeal depiction: that we depict before us ten circles, and in each and every circle ten faces, which are the ten aspects of the ten Sefirot that are in each one of the ten Sefirot; and the faces revolve, face opposite face, as their rule requires. For example: the face of the Malkhut-within-Keter with the face of the Keter-within-Chokhmah, and so the Keter in them all with the Malkhut-within-Keter—for then the effluence is of another kind; and afterward we turn the face of the Yesod-within-Keter to the face of the Keter in them all—the effluence will be of [yet] another kind. And so for all the ten faces of Keter: there are ten kinds of effluence and ten kinds of channels, for according to the change of the effluence the channels change. And now, if we turn Chokhmah alone ten times, for each one of the ten faces of Keter, without the faces of the remaining Sefirot changing or turning, the number of the kinds of effluence will amount to one hundred.

And the matter of these divisions cannot be set down in writing; and if a person wishes to accustom himself to them, let him occupy himself with the figure depicted before him, and conduct himself in it with inquiry for many days, until YHVH enlightens the eyes of his intellect. For the power of the pen fails to prolong these matters further—unless this matter be passed on from mouth to mouth, or the discerning one delve into them with his intellect by means of this figure.

And behold, with this the Gate is concluded; and blessed is the true Helper, to whom wisdom belongs. And in these matters we fear error and trust in pardon; for of such as this it is said (Proverbs 5:19), "in her love you shall err [tishgeh] always"—these are matters which a person does not grasp except through difficulty.

<small>(Says the editor: These ten circles, in which the ten Sefirot are depicted—let the inquirer picture [them] as though the circles were revolving in their rotation, and then he will understand the intent of the author, peace be upon him. And the matter is: when the inquirer examines the facing of the Sefirot—for example, the aspect of the Chokhmah-within-Chokhmah to the aspect of the Chokhmah-within-Keter, or the aspect of the Binah-within-Binah to the aspect of the Binah-within-Chokhmah or within Keter—then he must imagine and think as though the circle revolves and the Chokhmah-within-Chokhmah, in the circle of Chokhmah, stands opposite the Chokhmah that is in the circle of Keter; and so all of them. Then he will understand and discern the intent of the author, and will know it in truth, with the help of the God of knowledges, YHVH. Thus far [his] words):</small>
The Eighth Gate: Essence and Governance.

After we occupied ourselves in the preceding Gate with the matter of the channels in all the particulars of their parts, we have seen fit to explain in this Gate the matter of the Sefirot in their essence as it is apprehended by us—whether lovingkindness [Chesed], or judgment [Din], or mercy [Rachamim]—and something of the way of their governance, as far as is apprehended by us.
Chapter One:

Most of the Kabbalists have agreed that the Sefirot are a power that includes many opposites. And the parable for this is the will of the soul: for it turns to many actions, even if they are almost opposite—such as love and hatred, and anger and laughter, and the other opposite actions like these. And so is the matter in the Sefirot, which have in them judgment and mercy: at times [a Sefirah] clothes itself in judgment, and at times in mercy. And just as it is in the hand of a person to receive and to bestow—and each of these two actions divides into two: whether receiving good or receiving evil, whether bestowing good or bestowing evil—and likewise many [other] actions; and it is a small limb in a person, conducting itself according to the will of the soul: so is the matter of the Sefirot. There is in each and every Sefirah the power to effect a thousand thousands of thousands of differing actions, each and every one according to its matter and its power and its apprehension and its knowledge and its nature, which the Emanator impressed in it. And we know that this premise which we have set forth will be difficult for the inquirer, and he will say: if so, one Sefirah would have sufficed—why did He emanate ten, since the one is a power that includes many opposites, and by it He could effect all the actions? And to this we answer that they were needed for the reason explained in the Gate of the Reason for the Emanation, in chapter six: that for a human being to apprehend the hidden—that is to say, the Godhead—this revelation was needed, up to ten revelations, one below another, so that by this means the creatures might apprehend a little of the knowledge of the exaltedness of the Emanator.

And further: even though we say that there is in each Sefirah a power that includes many opposites, nonetheless there are still many things such that what this one pours forth, that one does not pour forth—as they, of blessed memory, said (Mo'ed Katan, fol. 28): "Children, life, and sustenance—the matter does not depend on merit, but the matter depends on mazal." And the meaning is: "merit" is Chesed, and "mazal" is Keter. And the intent is that, although most of the kindnesses and the good things are drawn from Chesed, and its name proves it, nonetheless children, life, and sustenance are not in the hand of this attribute; rather, their principal [source] is in Keter, for it is the supernal mazal. And even though the commentators explained otherwise and said that "merit" is Gevurah, nonetheless [it is] in accordance with these words of ours [that] it is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 10, fol. 24), and as we shall explain in the Gate of the Values of the Allusions, under the heading "merit." And in this way we shall explain that Binah receives those who return; therefore it is called Repentance [Teshuvah]. And it is there that pardon and atonement principally depend, by the power of the supernal Keter that overflows upon it. And in this way vengeance is in Gevurah; and so various actions are assigned to the Sefirot, and what is assigned to this one is not assigned to that one. And what was said above, that it is a power that includes many opposites, will be in this way: that in the action that is drawn from it, it must effect many opposites—like the eye, whose action is sight, yet it includes opposites: evil sight or good sight, little sight or much sight. And so is the matter in the Sefirot. The example of this: one who returns to YHVH with all his power and with all his intent, like the repentance of King David, peace be upon him, and all the other penitents who returned to YHVH with all that is possible within the bounds of repentance—these, certainly, their repentance is superior and is most accepted, to raise their soul to the choice grade that belongs to penitents. And when the sinner does not return to YHVH in this grade, then his repentance is accepted, but his soul will not ascend to that choice grade to which the repentance of King David, peace be upon him, ascended. And likewise one who returns and mortifies his soul with a slight mortification; and there is one who confesses his sin only; and likewise one who does not return until the crushing of the soul. And such things, which exist in parts of parts, the knowledge of human beings cannot encompass—only the divine knowledge and power, which belong to Him, may He be blessed and exalted, in the Sefirot. And all these divisions are for good, and to reward with good reward in the World to Come. And there is likewise, in this way, [the power] to punish one who did not afflict himself on Yom Kippur with the five afflictions that depend on Yom Kippur, which is Binah, certainly. For it is not fitting to punish one who ate to his fill as one who ate an olive's bulk or two olives' bulk; and one who ate and drank is not equal to one who had marital relations; and likewise one who had marital relations is not equal to one who anointed himself. And such are the distinctions that occur in reality, which human knowledge cannot encompass, still less judge—only the divine power.

And the matter of the negative commandments and the positive is that they are divided and dependent upon all ten Sefirot. And although all of them in their generality are the 248 positive commandments in Chesed and the 365 negative commandments in Gevurah, nonetheless their particulars are in the ten Sefirot, as we have said. And their punishment, or their reward, or their claim in judgment, or the rectification of the ruin that the sinner has ruined, depends upon the Sefirah to which the commandment alludes. And its particulars and its laws and its reward and its punishment, in general and in particular, are [by] the power that includes many opposites, of which we have spoken. For if it were a power specific to the Sefirah and fixed in it, then if it does good it would not punish, and if it punishes it would not do good; and if it increases reward for one it would not lessen [it] for others, and if it lessens [it] for one it would not increase [it] for others. Rather, certainly, it is compelled that they be a power that includes opposites, to judge the sinner or to reward the doer, whether little or much. And all these actions are by the will of the Emanator, who pours His providence upon them and by means of His Sefirot, as we explained in the Gate of Self and Vessels. And in this way is the governance in the world. And the question does not arise, to say: let all the commandments be in one power, and the judging itself in that power—for several reasons, [among them] the reasons that I explained in the Gate of the Reason for the Emanation and that we explained above.

And further: because it is not the commandments that necessitated the Sefirot, but the Sefirot that necessitated the commandments. For in our doing the commandment we unite the power that alludes to the commandment, which is a branch of the Sefirah, with its root; and this is the will of our Maker, that we unite His Sefirot—for by their light we see light, for in them is His Self—and it is the glory of the kingship of the [King of the] world that we rectify His palaces and His thrones as is fitting, so that His Shekhinah may be among us. And in some of the commandments there is power to remove the spirit of impurity from the earth, "and the idols shall be utterly cut off"; and this is the glory of the King of the world, that we contend with those who rise up against Him. And concerning this the Sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin, fol. 111): "'and opened her mouth without measure [chok]'—[this is] one who has not fulfilled even one statute [chok]," which is one commandment: even though he has not transgressed a negative commandment, nonetheless he has no portion in His attributes, may He be blessed, since he has not rectified or united there any attribute so that he might cleave to it. We can further answer, on that reason, in another manner, more seemly and acceptable: that the matter of the Sefirot is the revelation of His powers, which are His effects and are included in His Self, as will be explained further in the Gate of the Tzachtzachot; and this is for the sake of the governance. And lovingkindness and mercy and might and victory and thanksgiving and righteousness and kingship—all of them are attributes included in Him and hidden in His Self. And no multiplicity befalls the Emanator by this, God forbid, as we explained in the Gate of the Order of the Emanation, and we shall also explain in the Gate of the Tzachtzachot, in chapters three [and] four. And now, will the questioner ask why a person has made, in his garment, sleeves, or leggings, or sheaths for the digits? No. For we shall answer him that, since this is the garment for the body, and the body is the cause of the garment, it is compelled that the garment be correlated with the body in all its parts and in all its limbs. And since the Sefirot are the revelation of His attributes, and are a garment to them, as we explained in the Gate of Self and Vessels, in chapter four—if so, the question does not arise, "why thus and not thus," as we have said.

And behold, in this way it has been explained how the question does not arise concerning the human body—why its limbs are thus and not thus, and why its hairs are thus, and all such things. For the body is a garment to the soul, and the soul reveals its actions by means of it—so much so that when [a person] sins and is defiled, that sin is depicted in the soul and afterward in the body, as the prophet testified in his reproofs (Isaiah 3), "The look of their faces testifies against them," etc. And so it says in the Zohar that at a time when there is pestilence in the city, God forbid, it is fitting for every person to cover his forehead, so that the Angel of Death not recognize his iniquities engraved on his forehead. And so the Sages, of blessed memory, said (Ta'anit, fol. 30b): "Whoever eats meat and drinks wine on the eve of the Ninth of Av—his iniquities are engraved upon his bones, as it is said, 'and their iniquities were upon their bones.'" And all this is for the reason that the soul shows its actions in them, and the stains that are in it, it shows in the body.

And behold, it is known that the soul is composed of ten, as we explained in the Gate "Ten and Not Nine," chapter five, and as will be explained in the Gate of the Soul. And since the soul is composed of all the upper worlds, it is compelled that its garment be the mold and form of the soul, which is the form of the upper worlds. And this is what Scripture says (Job 19:26): "and from my flesh I behold God." If so, it turns out, accordingly, that it is compelled that its limbs be in this structure, and [with] these joints and these veins, which are the channels of the effluence that is poured to the limbs. And all these limbs [matters] are verified of themselves and need no proof; and they will be explained at length in the Gate of the Soul, in part two.
